sentence: sometimes at 3am i think about how the moon has been watching everyone i've ever loved sleep and that feels like the most intimate thing in the world. like the moon knows my mother's face when she dreams. the moon knows what my exes look like with their guards down. it's the only witness to all of us.

i keep thinking about the version of me that exists in someone's mind who hasn't talked to me in five years. she's frozen at 22. she still wears that yellow sweater. she still believes everything will be okay. i kind of envy her honestly. she doesn't know any of this yet.

weird how grief works. you'll be fine for months and then a stranger on the bus laughs the same way your grandmother did and suddenly you're nineteen again in her kitchen and she's still alive and the soup is still on the stove and nothing bad has happened yet.

do you ever think about how every single person you walk past has had their heart broken at least once. every single one. the woman at the grocery store. the man on the train. the kid working the register. all of them carrying it. somehow we just keep walking around doing errands.

i wish someone had told me that healing isn't linear and also it isn't really healing. it's just learning to carry it differently. like a heavy bag you used to drag and now you can shoulder. you're stronger but the bag is the same weight. nobody warns you about that part.

the saddest thing about getting older is realizing your parents were just making it up as they went along. they were scared too. they were figuring it out in real time with you as the experiment. and now you're the age they were and you understand and you can't even be angry anymore.

there's a specific kind of loneliness that only exists at 4am when you can hear the trash trucks starting their route. like the city is waking up without you. like everyone has a place to be except you. like you've been left behind in some quiet apocalypse that only you noticed.

you can love someone with your whole chest and still not be able to live with them. you can know someone is wrong for you and still want them. you can outgrow people who never did anything wrong. love isn't always enough. that's not a tragedy. it's just how it is sometimes.

i romanticized sadness for so long because it was the only thing that felt real to me. happy felt like lying. content felt like settling. now i'm trying to learn that calm isn't boring. that peace doesn't mean i've given up on something. it just means i've stopped fighting myself.

thinking about how you can know someone for ten years and then they move away and slowly you become strangers again. you become a name they have to explain to new friends. you become a story. you become a memory. and they become that for you too. and somehow that's not the saddest thing.

ok so update. i went to that thing. it was fine. it was actually kind of good?? like i didn't want to be there but then maya showed up and we ended up sitting outside talking for like two hours about nothing. i think i needed it more than i realized. anyway. how was your day. tell me everything.

i can't stop thinking about what you said yesterday about how we always pick people who can't choose us back. i've been thinking about it all day at work. it's making me look at every relationship i've ever had through a different lens and i don't love it but i think you're right. ugh. you're always right.

wait you're not gonna believe this. i ran into david at the coffee shop. like *the* david. and he was with someone. and she had bangs. like the bangs he said he hated when i wanted to get them. i'm not even mad i'm just laughing. tell me you're laughing too because otherwise i'm going to cry.

ok hear me out. what if instead of going to the wedding we just rented a cabin somewhere and turned our phones off for three days. i'm so tired. i don't want to do small talk. i don't want to dance to taylor swift with strangers. i want to be in pajamas with you watching bad movies. please consider.

i'm so glad you called me last night. i'm sorry i wasn't more useful. i just kept thinking about how i wished i could drive over there and sit on your kitchen floor with you. anyway. did you eat today. have you had water. tiny things first. then we'll figure out the rest. love you.

the cat just knocked over my entire glass of wine onto the white couch. like deliberately. like she made eye contact first. she is the villain of this story and yet i still love her. i'm sending you a picture because i need someone else to witness this. she is unrepentant. she looks proud.

i had the weirdest dream that we were back in college and you were trying to convince me to drop out and move to lisbon with you. and in the dream i actually said yes. and we packed and went to the airport and then i woke up and felt sad we weren't actually there. is this a sign. should we move to lisbon.

remind me why i agreed to this dinner with my mom's friend's daughter. like why am i meeting strangers for networking dinners. i'm so bad at this. send me an excuse to leave at 8:30 so i can come over to your place and decompress. i'll bring wine. i'll bring the good wine. please.

ok so the therapist said i need to start telling people what i actually want instead of waiting for them to figure it out. so. i want to see you this weekend. i want you to come over and we can make that pasta and watch movies. i'm practicing. how am i doing. be honest. but gently.

do you remember the night we slept in your car outside that diner because we were too drunk to drive and too poor for a hotel. i was thinking about that today. how easy it used to be to just decide to do something stupid together. i miss when we had time to be stupid. let's plan to be stupid again soon.

this zine is for the girls who cry in target. this is for the boys who write poems in the notes app and never show anyone. this is for everyone who thinks they're too much and also somehow not enough. you are. and you aren't. and we love you here.

issue twelve. theme: rotting. what we mean by rotting: the slow soft decay of summer fruit on a windowsill. the way memory works. the way we let ourselves go in good ways. the way old houses smell. submissions are open. send us your blurry photos of your unmade bed.

a love letter to the corner store on hawthorne. to the cat that sleeps in the window. to the cashier who never remembers my name but always nods. to the bad coffee at the back. to the magazines i never buy. to the lottery tickets i never win. you are my church. you are my morning prayer.

things we are tired of: the word girlboss. capitalism in general. the idea that productivity is a moral category. people who don't tip. people who do tip but then talk about it forever. cold cities. things we love: pomegranates. the smell of old books. crying with a friend. dyeing your hair badly.

interview with marisol who runs the bookstore on elm. she has been there for thirty-one years. her hands are stained with ink. her cat is named after a dead poet. she said the secret to running a small business is to not really care about the money. she said this while laughing. we love marisol.

a manifesto for tired people. you are allowed to rest. you are allowed to not finish things. you are allowed to abandon hobbies. you are allowed to be inconsistent. you are allowed to be a different person from the one you were yesterday. you are allowed to be exactly the same person if you want.

i made this issue in two weeks of fevered productivity at my kitchen table. there's coffee on page seven. there's a fingerprint on page twelve. there are typos. i don't care. this is a handmade thing and handmade things have evidence of the hand. i hope you read it on a porch somewhere. i hope a moth lands on it.

things to do this autumn instead of being on the internet: collect dead leaves. press them in books you'll never reread. write a letter to someone you miss and don't send it. learn the names of three trees in your neighborhood. eat a soft pear standing at the kitchen sink. sleep with the window open.

we got a letter from a reader in oslo. they said our zine made them feel less alone in a way they couldn't explain. they said they read it on the bus and cried a little. they sent us a pressed flower in the envelope. we taped it to the wall above the desk. we are crying about it still.

a zine is the opposite of an algorithm. it is slow. it is specific. it is made by hands you will never see. it arrives in your mailbox crumpled. it gets a coffee ring on it. you give it to a friend and they keep it in their bedside drawer. it doesn't go viral. it just goes. somewhere. into the world.

ok so i've been making sourdough for about six months now and i finally feel like i know what i'm doing. mostly. the trick i didn't see anyone mention is that the temperature of your kitchen matters way more than any recipe says. like, my kitchen runs cold in winter, and the dough just sulks. i moved the proof to the top of the fridge. game changer. anyway here's the recipe.

hi friends, sorry it's been a while. life happened. dog had surgery, i had a deadline, my mom came to visit, the basement flooded a little. you know. the usual chaos. anyway i wanted to share what i've been reading lately because reading has been the only thing keeping me sane. quick reviews below. nothing fancy.

today i'm sharing my favorite cheap weeknight dinner. it's basically just rice, beans, an egg on top, hot sauce, and whatever vegetable is dying in the crisper. that's it. that's the recipe. i make a version of this probably twice a week. it's never disappointing and it costs like three dollars. you're welcome.

i tried to do a no-buy month and i lasted exactly nineteen days before i caved and bought a vintage lamp at a yard sale for eight dollars. i'm not even sorry. it has a little ceramic owl on the base. it brings me so much joy. i don't think i'm cut out for no-buy challenges. i'm more of a buy-less-stuff-thoughtfully person.

the garden update nobody asked for: the tomatoes are finally coming in. the zucchini has gotten completely out of control as zucchini does. i have given some to every neighbor on the block and they are now hiding when they see me coming. the basil bolted. the carrots are short and stubby but they taste fine. i call this a win.

thoughts on turning thirty: it's actually fine. i was kind of dreading it but the day came and went and nothing dramatic happened. i still don't know what i'm doing. i still call my mom when i'm sick. i still cry at commercials. the only difference is i go to bed earlier now and i'm extremely at peace with this development.

we took the kids to the lake this weekend and i forgot how exhausting traveling with small humans is. we spent more time loading and unloading the car than actually being at the lake. but they had fun. they have no memory of the chaos. only of the swimming. that's a lesson in there somewhere. i'm too tired to write it.

five things i'm into this month: a podcast about old buildings, the new tracy chapman documentary, a brand of chili crisp my coworker introduced me to, a really specific shade of olive green, and a wool sweater i thrifted that i suspect was knit by someone's grandmother. life is small joys lately. i'm okay with that.

we finally finished painting the bedroom. it took three weekends. there are now two coats of a color called soft fern on the walls. i love it. my partner thinks it looks slightly hospital-ish but is being supportive. before pictures and after pictures below. ignore the unmade bed in the after photos. i'm not staging this for anyone.

i started swimming again after like a decade away from it and i forgot how good it feels to be tired in your whole body. like a deep clean tired. the kind that makes you sleep like the dead. i'm not fast. i'm not graceful. but i go three mornings a week and i think i might actually be becoming a person who exercises. weird.

monday. didn't sleep well. the cat woke me at 4 and i couldn't get back. spent the morning irritable and trying to hide it from everyone. ate a yogurt. went for a walk at lunch. felt slightly better. tomorrow i'll go to bed earlier. that's the plan. that's always the plan.

wednesday. saw my therapist. she said something that's been rattling around all day: that the people who hurt me weren't doing it because i deserved it, they were doing it because they were hurt. it doesn't fix anything. but it loosens something. i can feel it. like a knot starting to give.

saturday. went to the farmer's market with sam. bought too many tomatoes. ate one in the car like an apple. it dripped down my chin. sam laughed. i felt seventeen years old in the best way. there's so much joy in small things. i forget. i need to remember. i'm writing it here so i remember.

thursday. bad day. nothing happened. just the static kind of bad. couldn't focus at work. snapped at the dog for nothing. cried in the shower. ate cereal for dinner. some days are like this. tomorrow is allowed to be different. i'm going to bed now. trying not to be too hard on myself about it.

tuesday. mom called. she sounded tired. she's been doing too much for everyone as usual. i told her she's allowed to rest. she said she'll rest when she's dead. i hated that. i told her that. she laughed. we are not great at hard conversations. but at least we had one. that's something. that's something.

sunday. lazy day. didn't get out of bed until noon. read a whole novel cover to cover. ate toast in bed. the dog slept across my legs and i pretended i couldn't move. i needed this. i didn't realize how much i needed this. monday is coming but for now it isn't. for now there's just this. and that's enough.

friday. anniversary of dad's death. nine years. i thought it would be easier by now. it isn't really. it's just different. i made his pasta sauce for dinner. it tasted like him. i cried into it a little. i ate it anyway. that probably means something. that probably means he's still here in some way.

wednesday. found an old photo of me at twelve. i'm holding a fish i caught. i look so proud. so unselfconscious. i want to protect her. i want to tell her about all of it. i want to tell her none of it. i want to let her have the fish and the sun and the unbroken heart. i love her. i love her.

monday. trying to start over. new notebook. fresh page. that always feels good for about two weeks and then i lose track of it. but two weeks of writing is more than zero weeks. so. here we go again. hello journal. it's me. nothing's really different. but i'm trying. and that counts.

thursday. quiet good day. coffee on the porch. read for an hour before work. didn't check my phone until i was already at my desk. felt like a small rebellion against the way everything is. i want more days like this. i'm going to try. i'm going to keep trying. small. quiet. mine.

every time i open the dishwasher to find clean dishes i feel like i won a small game that nobody else is playing. and every time i open it to find dirty dishes i feel personally betrayed by past me. domestic life is mostly just being in conflict with yourself across time.

the older i get the more i think the secret to happiness is just having a couple of friends you can be ugly with. not pretty-ugly. ugly-ugly. the kind where you don't shower before they come over. the kind where you say the embarrassing thing first. that's it. that's the whole secret.

society wants me to have hobbies and also wants me to be productive at all times. and the people who say find a hobby are the same people who later ask how it's monetizing. let me knit a bad scarf in peace please. let me garden badly. let me have a hobby that is actively bad.

fascinating that we as a species decided to invent the open floor plan and then also invent loud appliances and then act surprised when our kitchens and living rooms are unbearable. you can hear someone microwaving leftovers from three rooms away. this is not a triumph of design. this is a war crime.

i am once again thinking about how the phrase i'll sleep when i'm dead is something only people who have not yet experienced really good sleep would say. sleep is the best thing. sleep is the point. i want to sleep so well that when i die i'll be disappointed i don't get to do it anymore.

i refuse to believe that anyone actually likes the produce section at trader joe's. those plastic bags. the cilantro that's already wet and dying. the avocados in their threatening little net. and yet i go back. i go back every week. i don't know what's wrong with me. i'm part of the problem.

every airport is just a giant casino for stressed people. there are no clocks. there are flashing screens. the lighting is bad on purpose. they sell you twelve dollar wine. they make you walk past every duty free counter. they want you to buy the toblerone. they're going to win. they always win.

if you have a friend who texts you back within an hour you actually have nothing to complain about. i text back in three to five business days. i love my friends. i think about them constantly. i just don't text them. this is my flaw. i'm aware. i'm working on it. i'm probably not actually working on it.

stop telling me to romanticize my life. i was already romanticizing my life. now you've made it weird. now i'm self-conscious about how i drink my coffee. now i can't just look out a window without performing it. let me look out the window unobserved. let me have a small life with no audience.

people who say children's books are easy to write have never tried to write a children's book. there are no spare words. every sentence has to be perfect. you have to be funny and tender and not condescending and also pleasant to read aloud at bedtime for the eight hundredth time. it is the hardest writing there is.

dear seventeen-year-old me. you don't know this yet but the boy in the green hoodie is not going to be the love of your life. he is going to be a story you tell at parties. you are going to laugh about him. it's going to be fine. you are going to be so much more than this. please don't worry. please eat lunch.

dear twenty-three-year-old me. i know you think you have to figure out your career right now. you don't. nobody does. the people who seem to are lying or rich. you are going to switch fields three times and somehow that will turn out to be the right move. please stop checking linkedin at 2am. please go outside.

dear nine-year-old me. you were right about your gut feeling on miss carter. she really did not like you and it really wasn't your fault. you were not a bad kid. you were not weird. you were a fine kid. she was just tired and in the wrong job. you didn't deserve to be made to feel small. you deserved better.

dear thirty-year-old me. you're going to think you wasted your twenties. you didn't. you learned a lot of things. mostly about who you are not. that's still useful. that's still progress. stop looking back at it with so much disgust. she was doing her best. she was scared all the time. give her some credit.

dear fifteen-year-old me. about your body. i'm so sorry for all the things you said to it in the mirror. it was carrying you through something hard. it deserved kindness. it still does. one day you will look at photos from this year and you will not believe how beautiful you were. you couldn't see it then. i can see it now.

dear twenty-six-year-old me. you should leave that job. you know it's bad. you know it's hurting you. you're going to leave eventually but you're going to lose a year of your life first being miserable. please leave sooner. please believe me. there are other jobs. you are not stuck. you have never been stuck.

dear eleven-year-old me. about the journal you hid under the mattress. your mother found it. she didn't say anything because she didn't know how. she's sorry. she's been sorry for twenty years. she just didn't have the words. she loved you. she loves you. it was complicated. it wasn't your fault. nothing was your fault.

dear twenty-year-old me. i know you think your roommate hates you. she actually has anxiety. she will tell you this in three years over coffee. she will apologize for being distant. you will both cry a little. you will become friends again. please don't write her off. please don't be so quick to assume.

dear twenty-eight-year-old me. i know you are very angry at your father right now. you are right to be. you also need to know that he will die when you are thirty-four and you will not have made up. you will live with that. it will be okay. but. but. but. think about calling him. just think about it.

dear six-year-old me. you are going to love so many things in your life. a black cat. a book about a horse. a song your aunt sings at thanksgiving. a small green dress. a creek behind a friend's house. you are going to be okay. i know things are loud at home. but you are going to be okay. i promise.

i wrote his name on the back of my math notebook in pencil so i could erase it if anyone asked. i practiced our combined initials. i looked up the meaning of his name in a book. i told nobody. nobody. it was the most important secret of my life. he didn't know i existed. it didn't matter. it absolutely didn't matter.

she had a chipped front tooth from a softball injury and i thought about that tooth for years. i thought about that tooth at my own wedding to someone else. i thought about that tooth at her funeral. she was sixteen when i fell in love with her. she was seventy-three when she died. some things you just carry forever.

his name was elliot and he had freckles across his nose like the milky way and i was eleven and i did not know what to do with the feeling that he gave me. it felt like swallowing a small bird. it felt like running a fever. i still don't have a better word for it. i don't think there is one.

i loaned him my favorite book and he never gave it back. i still don't have it. i could buy another copy. i never have. it feels like the loss is the point now. it feels like if i replaced it i would be erasing what happened. and what happened was: i loved him and he didn't notice and he kept my book.

we sat next to each other in band class. she played flute. i played clarinet. once she handed me a bobby pin from her hair because mine had come loose and i thought i might actually die from the casual intimacy of it. i kept that bobby pin in a small box for four years. i probably still have it somewhere.

in seventh grade i was so in love with daniel that i would walk a longer way to class just to pass his locker. he didn't know my name until april. when he finally said hi to me in the hallway i could not respond. i just walked into the wall. i actually walked into the wall. he laughed. it was the best moment of my life so far.

she was a substitute teacher for one week in fifth grade and i wrote a poem about her hair. i still remember the poem. i'm not going to write it here because it was bad. but the point is i was nine years old discovering metaphor for the first time and her hair was the catalyst and i think that's beautiful.

his last name was hernandez and i used to whisper it to myself like a prayer. i was twelve and catholic and very confused about feelings in general. i prayed for him every night and also prayed to stop praying for him. neither prayer was answered. he moved away in the fall. i was free. i was devastated.

we slow danced at the eighth grade dance to a song i now actively dislike. i remember thinking i could feel his heartbeat through his shirt and that was the most adult thing that had ever happened to me. he was probably just sweating. i was probably also just sweating. we never spoke again after that summer.

she asked me to sign her yearbook and i wrote three sentences and erased them four times before settling on have a good summer with a smiley face. i was incapable of saying i love you i love you i love you. i still think about what i could have written. i still think about it twenty years later. that's how love works i guess.

soft october sunday. coffee on the porch. the cat in the window. the leaves doing their slow yellow business. nothing to report. nothing to sell you. just a small life happening in real time. i think this is what they call contentment. i think i'm finally home.

made it back from portland in one piece. ate too many oysters. walked too many miles. saw three rainbows in one day. cried at a bookstore. fell asleep on a couch in a stranger's apartment. drove home with the windows down. would do it all again tomorrow if you asked me.

thirty-four years on this planet. still figuring it out. still laughing too loud in restaurants. still crying at country songs in the car. still in love with the same person somehow. thank you to everyone who texted today. thank you for being here. another year please.

the bread came out lopsided. i ate it anyway. it tasted like victory. it tasted like time. it tasted like the kitchen of my grandmother who taught me nothing about bread because she didn't bake but who would have been proud of the lopsidedness because she was a lopsided woman who loved me very much.

found this little guy at the shelter today. his name is otis. he's nine years old. he was returned twice. he sleeps with his tongue out. he is not going anywhere ever again. welcome home buddy. you're stuck with me now. this is going to be the best worst thing i ever did.

trying not to post too much about the wedding because it was honestly just a really good party with the love of my life. that's all it was. nothing fancy. nothing curated. we got married in the backyard. there was barbecue. the dog wore a tie. it rained for ten minutes. it was perfect.

five years ago today i was in a hospital. i was twenty-eight pounds lighter. i did not think i would make it to thirty. now i am thirty-two. now i am running 5ks. now i am eating lunch every day. thank you to the people who stayed. you saved my life. i don't say that lightly.

first frost this morning. the basil is dead. the marigolds are clinging on. the dog refused to go outside until i bribed him with a piece of cheese. the kitchen smells like coffee and toast. i lit a candle even though it isn't dark yet. autumn is a religion in this house. you can't fight it.

studio update. finished a piece i've been working on for six months. i don't know if it's good. i don't know if anyone will buy it. i don't really care today. i care that i finished it. i care that i kept showing up. that has to count for something. that has to be enough sometimes.

swipe to see my favorite picture of my mom from this trip. she is laughing at something i said. she is wearing a hat she bought at a gas station. she is sixty-eight years old. she is more beautiful now than in any picture from her twenties. i hope when i am her age i look this happy.

today was the worst day of my entire life. i can't even talk about it. okay i'll talk about it. so jenna and emma had a sleepover and didn't invite me. and they posted about it. and they didn't even apologize when i asked. and now i don't know if i have any friends at all. i hate everyone. i hate myself. i hate this school.

i think i might be in love with sam. like actual love. like the kind people write songs about. we sat next to each other at lunch and he asked me what i was reading and we talked for forty minutes about nothing. i could not eat my sandwich. i could barely breathe. i went home and laid on my bed and stared at the ceiling for two hours.

my mom is being so unfair. she said i can't go to the concert because i got a c on my chemistry test. like that's not even my fault chemistry is impossible. i hate her. okay i don't hate her. but i'm really mad. she doesn't understand that this is the biggest concert of my life. i'm going to die if i don't go.

the dance was so weird. nobody danced for like the first hour. then the lights went down and suddenly everyone was a different person. i don't know what happened but at one point i was slow dancing with three different people in a circle and that's not even how dancing works. i had so much fun. i don't know who i am.

i told my dad i wanted to be a writer when i grow up and he said writing is a fine hobby but i should pick a real job. i am not speaking to him for the rest of my life. or at least until tomorrow. i'm going to be a writer. i'm going to be famous. and then he'll be sorry. and then i won't even care.

i can't sleep. i keep thinking about the universe. like really thinking about it. like how it just keeps going forever and ever and we're on this tiny little planet and we're just going to die and nobody will remember any of this. and then i thought about it for too long and now i'm scared and i need to stop thinking about the universe.

spent all afternoon making a mixtape for ryan. then deleted it. then made it again. then changed two songs. then deleted it again. then made it again. i don't know how anyone confesses feelings to another human being it is literally impossible. i think i'll just continue to suffer in silence forever. that seems easier.

best day of my life. ryan asked me to homecoming. he just walked up to me at my locker and said do you wanna go and i said yes before he even finished asking. so we're going. as a date. i need a new dress. i need to learn how to walk in heels. i need to calm down. i can't calm down. i won't calm down.

i think my parents are going to get divorced. they're being weird. they're polite to each other but it's the kind of polite that strangers are. they're not even fighting anymore. i think the not-fighting is worse than the fighting. i don't know what to do with this information. i'm not telling anyone. i'm just writing it here.

today miss thompson kept me after class to ask if everything was okay at home. i don't know what i did to make her ask. i said yes everything's fine. i don't know if she believed me. i'm not sure if everything is fine. but i'm not going to talk to a teacher about it. that's not what teachers are for. or maybe it is. i don't know.

what struck me first about this piece is the way the negative space is doing more work than the positive space. that's rare. that's a real choice and not an accident. i'd push you to lean into it harder. give the eye more room to wander. don't be afraid of empty. empty is a material too.

i'm not convinced by the color palette here. it feels like you're playing it safe. earth tones are a hiding place. i want to see you take a risk. burn it down a little. there's a version of this painting that's bright and ugly and alive and i think you're scared of it. let yourself be scared and do it anyway.

the figure in the foreground is doing all the storytelling. but i keep coming back to the small window in the upper left corner. there's something happening in that window that i can't put words to and i can't stop looking at it. that's the painting. that's the heart of it. trust that instinct. follow it.

this series feels overworked to me. i can see every revision. every second-guess. every moment you almost gave up and kept going. that's not a compliment. the labor is showing through and it's drowning the image. step away. let the next one breathe. let yourself make something that isn't perfect on purpose.

there's a tenderness in the way you handle the hands in these portraits that i find genuinely moving. you understand hands. you understand what they say. the rest of the figure could be doing more but the hands are already telling the truth. start there next time. let everything else follow what the hands are doing.

the title is doing too much work. it's telling me what to feel. take the title off. let the piece survive on its own. if it can't survive without a title, that's information. that's the work telling you it isn't done yet. titles should be the last thing, not the first. titles are jewelry, not architecture.

i want to talk about why you keep choosing the same subject. it isn't a criticism. i think you haven't finished with this subject yet and that's okay. some painters spend their whole lives on one apple. one mountain. one face. there's no shame in that. but i want you to know that's what you're doing. own it. claim it. it's a choice.

the photographs from this trip are technically beautiful but emotionally distant. you're standing too far back. i want you closer to your subjects. i want you uncomfortable. the best documentary work happens when the photographer is implicated in the scene. you've been hiding behind the camera. come out from behind it.

i think the sculpture wants to be smaller. you've made it big because big feels important. but the gesture is intimate. it's a thing you'd hold in your hand. when you scaled it up you lost something. don't be afraid of small. small is a strength. small can be devastating. consider what this piece is at six inches.

the video has too much music. the music is doing the work the image should be doing. mute the whole thing. watch it silent. if it still works, you have a piece. if it doesn't, the music is the problem and you're using it as a crutch. silence is harder. silence is honest. try silence first.

logged on to write about my day but i can't really remember it. i made coffee. i answered emails. i ate a sandwich at my desk. i went on a walk. i came home. nothing happened. and yet i'm exhausted. and yet i feel like i need to log this somewhere. proof that today existed. proof that i was here.

had the friendship crisis again. the one where i think nobody actually likes me and they're all just being nice. went to therapy. she said my brain is a liar. i know my brain is a liar. but knowing your brain is a liar doesn't actually stop it from lying. anyway. i'm fine. mostly. tomorrow will be better. hopefully.

small joy report. found a beetle on the kitchen window today and let it outside instead of squishing it. felt smug about it for the rest of the morning. is that growth or is that just being a person who has time to deal with a beetle. either way. i'm logging it. i'm calling it a win.

the laundry has been in the dryer for two days. i know it's there. i'm not going to deal with it. someone will eventually deal with it. probably me. but not today. today i'm going to lie on the couch and read and pretend the laundry doesn't exist. this is what i call adult life. it is mostly procrastination with better lighting.

back from a week of being offline. i don't know what to report. i read three books. i ate breakfast outside every morning. i swam in cold water. i didn't think about anyone i'm supposed to be thinking about. i don't know if it changed anything. but i feel slightly more like myself. whatever that means.

weird week. i don't know how to describe it. i kept feeling like i was about to remember something important but couldn't quite get there. like the word was on the tip of my tongue but the word was actually an entire life decision. i think i might quit my job. or move. or both. but i'm not going to. probably. let's see.

current obsessions: the smell of woodsmoke. the song that goes hold on hold on hold on. cardamom in oatmeal. my own handwriting. a particular shade of dirty green. the way my partner laughs in their sleep. i don't know what this list means but i'm writing it down because someday i'll want to remember who i was right now.

we finally cleaned out the garage. found a box of letters my grandfather wrote to my grandmother during the war. they are unbelievably tender. they are unbelievably stupid in places. they are deeply themselves. i sat on the floor of the garage and read them for two hours. i cried twice. i'm glad we kept them. i'm so glad.

rainy day. did nothing. and i mean nothing. didn't shower. didn't brush my hair. ate cereal from the box. watched four hours of a baking show. felt no shame. felt no productivity. felt nothing at all. it was a kind of medicine i didn't know i needed. tomorrow i'll do the things. today is for sitting still.

i keep meaning to write here more often and then days go by and nothing gets written. i think it's because the small things feel too small and the big things feel too big. there's no middle. but actually maybe the small things are the whole point. so. small thing. the dog got groomed today. she looks ridiculous. she's so proud. that's it. that's the entry.

hey. just checking in. no need to respond. thinking of you today. saw a yellow bird on the way to work and thought of you specifically. don't know why. just did. hope you're okay over there. okay that's all. love you. bye.
running like ten minutes late. traffic on the bridge is wild. order me whatever you're having. and a water. and the bread. don't let them take away the bread. i'm almost there i promise.

ok the lab called. it's fine. it's all fine. don't worry. just wanted to tell you before you started worrying because i know you. take a breath. everything is normal. i'll explain when i get home tonight. love you. don't worry.

couldn't sleep. been awake since 3. thinking too much. i know you're at work right now. don't text back. just wanted somewhere to put the words. i'm okay. just one of those nights. talk later. love you. go sell that house.

i found the keys. they were in the freezer. don't ask. i don't know how they got there. but. found. crisis over. coming home now. love you. and yes i checked twice. they're definitely the right keys this time.
the funeral is wednesday at 2. you don't have to come. but if you can come. it would mean a lot. either way i love you. either way i know you're with me. that's enough. that's always enough.

happy birthday. i'm not gonna do the long sappy thing. you know what i'd say. you've heard it before. you'll hear it again. just know that another year of you on this planet is the only thing i actually celebrate. love you. let's get tacos this weekend.

ok genuinely freaking out about tomorrow. i know it's just a job interview. i know i'm qualified. i know all the things. and yet here we are. spiraling at 11pm. please send me a picture of your cat. urgent therapeutic emergency. thank you.

weather here is unreal. i wish you could see it. the kind of sky that doesn't look real. i took a picture and it doesn't capture it. you'd love it. you should be here. why aren't you here. fly out next weekend. just do it. say yes.

no need to call back. just wanted to say i was thinking about that thing you told me last summer about your dad. i think you were right about it. i think it took me a year to understand what you meant. anyway. you're smarter than you give yourself credit for. love you. bye.

songs for driving alone at night when you have nowhere to be. songs for crying in the bathtub. songs for missing someone you shouldn't miss. songs for sitting in the parking lot of your old high school when you're back in town. songs for endings that don't feel like endings yet.

this is a soundtrack for the first cold day of fall. for putting on a sweater that smells like last year. for staring out a window with a hot drink. for thinking about everyone you've loved. for being okay with the thinking. for letting the thinking be the whole point.

a playlist for the slow days. for the days when you wake up and don't know what year it is. for the days when nothing has to happen and somehow that's the hardest part. for the days when the light comes through the curtains and you're in love with your own quiet life.

broken-up but not over it. that's the vibe. that's the entire vibe. songs that aren't about your ex specifically but feel like they were written about your ex specifically. songs you can't listen to in public because you'll start crying on the bus. songs that are kind of bad but you love them anyway.

a winter playlist for staying in. for slow cooking something on a sunday. for reading a book in bed at three in the afternoon. for letting the day be small. for resisting the part of you that thinks rest is the same as laziness. it isn't. it never was.

songs i listened to that summer when everything was about to change but i didn't know it yet. when i was working that bookstore job. when i was in love with the wrong person. when i lived in that apartment with the green walls. when i thought i had time. before i knew what time was.

the playlist for grocery shopping at midnight. for the fluorescent lights. for the bored cashier. for the seven things in your basket that don't make a meal. for the walk back to the car. for the trunk slamming. for the long quiet drive home. for the radio just barely loud enough.

for the people who feel things too much. for the people who put songs on repeat for a week and don't get tired of them. for the people who text lyrics to other people who get it. for the people who would have been in the school band if they hadn't been so afraid of being seen. this one's for you. it always was.

a list for old houses. for creaky floors and slow plumbing. for windows that don't quite close. for porches and screen doors. for the smell of someone else's grandmother's kitchen. for being a guest in a town you used to live in. for being a ghost in your own old life.

a playlist for getting on a plane and not telling anyone where you went. for sitting in the airport at 5am with a too-hot coffee. for window seats. for the bad airplane wine. for the way the light hits the clouds when you're above them. for arriving somewhere new and not yet being yourself.

the dishwasher is making that sound again the one where it sounds like a small animal in distress and i don't have time to deal with it today and also i should be writing the report but i'm thinking about whether to get a haircut and whether i want bangs and whether bangs would make me look younger or just look like a person trying to look younger which is its own thing

what if everyone i've ever known had a version of me in their head and they all added up to who i am and i'm just the average of all those versions and there's no real me underneath just a kind of collective fiction held together by my body which is the only consistent thing across all those people's perceptions and even the body changes

okay so the thing is i wanted to be a painter when i was nine years old and then somewhere between nine and now i stopped painting and i'm not sure exactly when it happened but i think it might have been the third grade art teacher who told me my tree looked wrong and i never recovered from that and now i work in software which is fine but i'm not sure i ever decided to do this

the kitchen tile is the same kitchen tile that was in my grandmother's house and every time i walk on it barefoot i'm seven years old again and she's making sandwiches and the radio is on and the dog is sleeping under the table and i don't know any of the bad things yet and i can't tell if remembering this is comforting or devastating

everyone keeps asking what i want for my birthday and the honest answer is i want everyone i love to stop dying which is not something you can put on an amazon wish list so i just say a candle and they buy me a candle and i pretend that's what i wanted and we all move on with our lives until the next birthday

i'm trying to remember the name of the song that was playing in the car the night we drove home from the lake and i can hear the chorus in my head but i can't get to the words and it's been haunting me for three days and i refuse to look it up because if i find it that easily it won't mean anything anymore

thinking about how the same body that was twelve years old and could climb every tree in the backyard is the body i'm sitting in right now typing this and it has changed almost every cell and yet it remembers everything and that's a strange continuity to be made out of and i don't know how to think about it without getting dizzy

i forgot to call my mother on her birthday last year and i still think about it every single day and she said she didn't care but she did care and i know she did and i can't undo it and i call her every week now but it doesn't feel like enough and maybe nothing would feel like enough

the cat is staring at me again and i don't know what she wants she has food she has water she has a window to look out of and yet she stares and i wonder if she is judging the choices that have led me to this exact tuesday and frankly i would be too if i were her

every time i drive past the elementary school i feel a tug in my chest that i can't fully account for it isn't sadness it isn't nostalgia it's something more specific like the feeling of being small in a body that knew nothing yet and i don't know if i'd go back if i could but i think about it more than i should admit

the kitchen is too small for both of us. but we do it anyway. i chop. you stir. we bump elbows. you say sorry. i say sorry. the rice cooker is on the floor because there's no counter space. the cat is judging us from the windowsill. dinner will be good. dinner is always good. that's how we know we made it.

i made a soup tonight from things i didn't think went together and somehow it worked. carrot. lentil. lemon. cumin. a single old onion. some leftover ginger from a recipe i didn't finish. i ate two bowls. the apartment smells incredible. the bowl is still by the sink. i'll deal with it tomorrow.

no oven. one burner. a microwave that scares me. and yet. i made pasta. i made it on the burner. i stirred it with a wooden spoon i bought at goodwill. the sauce was from a jar but i added a thing of butter at the end and it tasted like a restaurant. small kitchens make you resourceful. or hungry. probably both.

my whole spice collection lives in a shoebox under the sink. labeled in sharpie. organized by which ones i actually use. cumin lives in the front. cardamom lives in the back. the bay leaves are in a ziplock. this is not how spice racks are supposed to work but it is how my spice rack works. and the food tastes the same.

i learned to bake bread in this apartment. on the rack of a toaster oven. i'm not kidding. the loaves come out small and dense but they are mine. i give them to my neighbors. one of them cried the first time. she said it reminded her of poland. i didn't have the heart to tell her i used a toaster oven.

the trick to a small kitchen is doing things in order. wash everything as you go. don't dirty a bowl if you can use a measuring cup. cook with one pan if at all possible. accept that you will eat standing up. accept that you might eat directly out of the pan. the food will still be good. you will still feed yourself. that's the whole point.

we had people over for dinner. four people. in this kitchen. i don't know how we did it. we did it. there was a stew. there was bread. there was wine. there was a candle stuck in an empty bottle for atmosphere. there was laughter. there were stories. the kitchen was tiny and the night was huge.

my favorite thing to cook on bad days is rice and an egg. you put a little oil in a pan. you crack an egg. you let the edges go crispy. you put the egg on the rice. you add soy sauce. you add hot sauce. you eat it with a spoon. it costs almost nothing. it tastes like home. it tastes like being okay.

the herbs grow on the windowsill. basil. parsley. a sad little oregano that refuses to die. i talk to them in the morning. don't judge me. they grow better when i talk to them. the basil is on its third generation. its great-grandparent was a plant from the grocery store in 2022. small kitchens have small empires.

i don't own a stand mixer. i don't own a food processor. i don't own a kitchenaid anything. i own one good knife and a wooden spoon my mother gave me when i moved out at twenty-two. and you know what. the food is fine. the food is great. you don't need stuff to cook. you need to be hungry and unafraid.

got a new haircut today. shorter than i meant. but the longer i look in the mirror the more i think this is who i was supposed to look like all along. spent two hours trying on flannel shirts at the thrift store. came home with three. the woman at the register said i looked like her son. i'm taking that as a compliment.

we held hands in the parking lot today. just for a second. just long enough that someone could have seen. and i wasn't scared. and that's new. and i want to write it down because it feels like a small revolution and i don't want to forget what the air felt like.

the boots came in the mail. they fit. they are heavier than i expected. they make me walk differently. they make me hold doors open. they make me carry things. i don't know if that's the boots or me but i like the version of myself who lives inside them. i'm not taking them off for a week.

my niece asked me today why i don't wear dresses. i said because i don't want to. she said that's a good reason. she's seven. she got it immediately. why do adults make this so complicated. why does anyone need a longer explanation. that's the explanation. that's the whole explanation.

my partner came home with flowers tonight. she said they reminded her of me. they were small and yellow and slightly crooked in the vase. and that's the most accurate thing anyone has ever said about how i present in this world. small and yellow and slightly crooked. i'm going to cry about this for like a week.

i taught my partner how to fix the sink today. she didn't need me to. she watched anyway. we ate dinner on the kitchen floor afterwards because the table was covered in tools. i don't know why i'm writing this down. it just felt important. it just felt like the kind of small ordinary night that adds up to a life.

the kids on the swim team called me coach today and i didn't correct them. i was supposed to. i'm not really their coach. i just help out. but coach felt right. and i'm going to think about that for the rest of the week. how a small word can land in your chest like a small key.

we drove out to the lake just to look at it. she made sandwiches. i made coffee. we sat on a blanket in the back of the truck and didn't talk for a long time. and when we did talk it was about nothing. and that was the point. and the dog slept between us. and the sun went down. and i thought yes. this. forever this.

i still get nervous in barbershops sometimes. like they're going to ask what i'm doing here. nobody ever does. they just ask how short. and i tell them. and they cut my hair. and it's fine. and afterward i sit in my car for a few minutes feeling lighter and i don't always know why.

spent the weekend at my parents' house. my mother said you look more like yourself than you used to. and i didn't know what to say. so i hugged her. and she hugged me back. and that's the most i've ever gotten from her about any of this. and it was enough. it was more than enough.

to the person who picked up my wallet on the bus last tuesday and turned it in to the driver with everything still inside: thank you. i don't know who you are. i don't know if i passed you on the street the next day. but you saved my week. you saved my month maybe. you are good. you are good and you should know it.

to the barista at the cafe on 5th who knows my order and asks how my mom is doing: i don't know how you remember any of us. i know you have your own life. but the way you make me feel seen at 8am on a wednesday is the closest thing i have to going to church. thank you. you do good work.

to the kid in my eighth grade english class who told me my poem was good. i don't remember your name. i don't think we ever talked again after that. but i'm a writer now and i think about that small kindness probably twice a year. it mattered. it really mattered. i hope you're doing well.

to the dog who lives on the corner of grand and 7th: i don't know your name. but every morning you bark at me when i walk past and every morning it makes me laugh. you are a small terrible joy in my life. you are extremely committed to your job. i salute you. i hope you live forever.

to the stranger who let me cut in line at the airport because she could see i was crying: you didn't have to do that. you didn't ask why. you just nodded. you let me through. and i made my flight and i got to my grandmother before she died and i don't know if you know what you did. but you did it. and thank you.

to my landlord who fixed the heater on christmas eve and refused payment: you are not what people say landlords are like. you are a saint. you are also extremely strange and we never talk and i don't know your life. but i hope yours is good. i hope someone is doing for you what you do for the rest of us.

to the strangers at my brother's funeral who said the things i needed to hear: i don't remember your faces. i barely remember my own face from those weeks. but the words you said are still in my chest. you didn't have to. nobody had to. but you did. and i'm telling you, even though you'll never read this: thank you.

to the mailwoman on our block: i know we drive you crazy with our packages. i know the dog still barks at you even though it's been four years. i know the steps are uneven and the address is hard to find at night. you are the most consistent presence in my life. you are also a hero. thank you for everything.

to the bus driver on the 47 line who hummed while he drove: i hope you're still humming. i hope you're driving still. i hope someone has told you how much the small things you do affect strangers. the city is colder now since you retired. or maybe you didn't retire. maybe you just moved routes. either way. thank you.

to my high school librarian who let me hide in the back room during lunch when i needed to: you saved a kid's life. you didn't know it. i didn't tell you. i was too embarrassed to tell you. but you did. and i'm a librarian now myself. and i think about you every time i unlock the doors. thank you.

started a new track this morning. just one held drone and a recording of rain i made out the kitchen window last november. i added a piano figure that goes nowhere. that's the whole piece. it's twelve minutes long. i don't know who it's for. probably for me. probably for one specific kind of afternoon.

the new album is called weather rooms. nine tracks, all between four and eleven minutes. recorded in my apartment during the longest winter i can remember. there are no drums. there are barely any words. there is a lot of breath. there is a piano with one broken key that i didn't fix. it sounds like home.

the trick to ambient music is doing less and less and less. every time i finish a piece i go back and remove three more elements. usually the piece is better. occasionally it falls apart. you have to be willing to let it fall apart. you have to be willing to make something that almost isn't.

i sampled the sound of my mother washing dishes for the closing track. i told her about it. she laughed and said i finally found a use for her. she has been washing dishes for sixty years. the sound is so specific. you can hear her hands. you can hear her breath. you can hear the whole kitchen.

the field recording was made at 4am in a parking lot outside seattle. i was on tour. i couldn't sleep. i went outside with my recorder and just stood there. you can hear a sprinkler somewhere. you can hear a train far off. you can hear the city not quite waking up. it's the best thing i ever recorded.

thinking a lot lately about silence as a compositional element. not the absence of sound. an active silence. the way a held note has a different quality when it's followed by space. the way space can ring. the way space can hurt. i'm trying to write a piece that's mostly silence. we'll see.

the live show last night went better than expected. i was nervous about playing such quiet music in a venue that usually hosts loud things. but the audience was patient. nobody talked. somebody cried in the front row. afterward she came up and said the second piece sounded like her grandmother. that's the best review i'll ever get.

i bought a tape machine. a real one. with reels. i don't know why. i don't need it. it's huge and it weighs nothing useful and it cost me a month of rent. but the sound it does to things. you can't fake it digitally. you can almost. but not quite. the not-quite is the point.

the album is finished. eighteen months of working on it. i still think it could be better. i'm going to release it anyway. that's the only way i learn anything. that's the only way the next one gets better. the worst thing a musician can do is be precious. i'm not being precious. i'm putting it out. now.

wrote a piece for cello and water glass tonight. i don't know if it's a piece. it might just be a sound. it might be the kind of thing i play once and then never play again. but for the duration of it tonight, while i was making it, i forgot i had a body. and that's the whole reason i do this.

the fiddle leaf fig is doing fine this week and i am refusing to celebrate because the moment i acknowledge it the plant will drop seventeen leaves out of spite. it has done this twice. it knows when i am happy. it cannot be allowed to know. we live in detente. i water it. i do not love it openly. it does not betray me.

the monstera put out a new leaf with no holes in it and i was personally offended. why am i feeding you. why are you taking up this much space. you had one job. the next one better come out properly fenestrated or you are going outside in a snowstorm. don't test me. i love you. but i will not be disrespected.

the pothos has taken over the entire bookshelf. it is now reaching toward the ceiling. i used to think i was the one in charge here. i was incorrect. the pothos lives here too. the pothos has opinions. the pothos is patient. one day i will come home and the pothos will be wearing my clothes. it's coming. i can feel it.

lost the orchid this week. it had two good years. it bloomed once. that was the highlight of my entire houseplant career. i'm not going to buy another one. i'm going to remember that one. that's enough. the orchid was a gift. orchids are always a gift. you don't keep them. you witness them.

the spider plant has babies again. there are now five hanging from it. they look like little chandeliers. they look like little punishments. i have to do something with them. i have to give them away. but to whom. who do i still know. who deserves a spider plant baby. this is a real question. someone please raise their hand.

i talk to the plants when i water them. i don't know if they like it. i don't know if i'm doing this for them or for me. but i say small things. how are you doing today little one. you're looking thirsty. is that a new leaf. i'm proud of you. it's the closest i come to praying. it's the only ritual i still keep.

the apartment has too many plants. there. i said it. there are too many. i don't have room for furniture. i don't have room for guests. i keep buying more. i don't know why. there's something deeply broken in me that needs to keep buying ferns. my therapist says it's about control. i think it's about life. she didn't disagree.

the basil has bolted. there's nothing to do. it's flowering now. it knows the season. it knows things i don't know. i'm going to let it flower. i'm going to let the bees come. i'm going to learn from it. about timing. about endings. about how a plant knows when its work is done. i don't know any of that yet.

my succulent collection is mostly stretched and sad. the apartment doesn't get enough light. they were a phase. i was twenty-four. i thought succulents would be easy. they are not easy if you live in a north-facing one-bedroom. they are dying slowly and i can't bring myself to throw them away. they came with me through two moves.

repotted everything this weekend. my hands are still smelling like dirt. the apartment looks like a botanical crime scene. i found a small spider in the prayer plant who has been living there for an unknown amount of time. i did not kill her. i moved her gently to the bathroom. she lives there now. her name is brenda.

ran four miles this morning and they were terrible. every step was negotiated. every breath was a complaint. and yet i finished. and yet the sky was pink at the turnaround point. and yet i'm sitting here drinking coffee feeling smug about myself. running is not about feeling good while running. running is about feeling good afterward. apparently.

race tomorrow. i'm not ready. i'm never ready. that's not the point. i ate pasta tonight. i laid out my clothes. i have my bib. i have my shoes. i have a small banana for the morning. now i'm going to lie awake until 3am thinking about every possible way the race could go wrong. that's also part of the training.

long run today. eighteen miles. the longest i've ever done. my watch died at mile thirteen. i kept going. i didn't know how to estimate distance after that. i just ran until my legs said stop. then i walked. then i ran again. then i was home. my partner was on the porch. she gave me water. she asked how it was. i said it was good. i meant it.

the running club met at 6am this morning. there were eight of us. four of us were strangers two months ago. now we know what each other's gait looks like in the half-dark. we know whose knees hurt this week. we know who needs a coffee after. running clubs are a kind of friendship i didn't know existed. it's quieter than other friendships. it's also deeper somehow.

missed a week of training because of the flu. felt sorry for myself for six days. on the seventh day i went outside and ran a slow easy three miles and remembered why i do this. it's not about the goals. it's about the going outside. it's about the breath. the goals are just an excuse to keep going outside.

set a small pr today. 5k in 24:38. for context: in 2019 i couldn't run a mile without stopping. i'm 38. i'm not a fast person. but i kept showing up. and now i'm a slightly less slow person. that's worth writing down. that's worth celebrating. that's the whole arc. small consistent showing up.

rain run this morning. nobody else was out. just me and the geese on the lake. the geese hate me. i hate them too. but we share the path. we have an understanding. i don't go near them. they hiss at me anyway. that's our relationship. that's how it's always been. i wouldn't have it any other way.

thinking a lot about pace lately. i used to be obsessed with going faster. now i'm obsessed with going for longer. i can run for two hours if i go slow enough. and during those two hours i think about everything. and nothing. and the things that have been bothering me dissolve. running slow is a kind of therapy. i'm just figuring this out.

marathon was yesterday. didn't hit my time goal. cried at mile twenty-two. finished anyway. crossed the line. ate a banana. cried again. called my mom. she said she was proud. i don't know if i'll do another one. i probably will. i always think i won't and i always do. i think i need the suffering. i think i'm wired wrong in a useful way.

running with the dog today went sideways. she saw a squirrel at mile two. she pulled me off the trail. i fell. she sat down and looked at me like i was the one being unreasonable. i was bleeding from my elbow. she licked my face. i couldn't be mad. she's a dog. i'm the one who clipped her to my waist. i am the architect of my own pain.

the diner on main street is run by a woman named darleen and she has been there since before i was born. she remembers my mother as a teenager. she remembers what my father always ordered. she calls everyone honey. she calls me honey when i visit. last time she had me in the back office for an hour telling me about her grandkids. i barely know her. i love her.

the courthouse in the middle of town has a clock that has been wrong for six years. it says 4:18. nobody fixes it. it has become a joke. it has become a landmark. people meet at the wrong clock. you tell visitors to meet at the wrong clock. the wrong clock is part of who we are now. don't try to fix it. we like it broken.

every spring the high school does the same musical they've been doing for thirty years. always grease. always the same teacher directing. always the same parents in the audience. and yet every year i go. and every year a different kid is sandy and it feels completely new. small towns are about the same thing happening forever with different people inside it.

the gas station out by the highway has the best fried chicken in the county. i'm not joking. i'm not exaggerating. people drive an hour to get this chicken. they fry it in lard. the woman who runs the kitchen learned it from her mother. her mother learned it from someone in mississippi. there's history in this chicken. it costs four dollars for two pieces. it's a miracle.

everyone in town drives a pickup or a subaru. there is no in between. you are one tribe or the other. you can switch tribes but you have to commit. you cannot drive a sedan. the sedan people don't come here. they don't last. the snow eats them by january. you have to commit to the truck or the subaru. those are the rules.

the library is open three days a week. the librarian is named martha. she has been reading the same novel for two years. she reads slowly. she reads carefully. she will not tell you the title. she says if you really want to know, you'll figure it out. i have not figured it out. i think about it constantly.

the volunteer fire department had their pancake breakfast on saturday. half the town came. the chief stood at the door collecting donations. nobody asked how much. people just gave what they had. some people gave hundreds. one kid gave a quarter. the chief shook his hand the same way. that's the town. that's the whole town in one moment.

we got a stoplight last year. the second one. people are still upset about it. it was a town meeting issue for three months. there were petitions. there were op-eds in the weekly paper. now it's just a stoplight. people sit at it. nobody talks about it anymore. that's how small towns absorb change. loudly. then completely.

the dog who lives at the hardware store doesn't have an owner exactly. he just lives there. they put a bed in the back. they feed him. he greets every customer. he is in the town newspaper twice a year. his name is steve. nobody knows why he's named steve. when steve dies the town is going to fall apart. don't think about it. just enjoy the steve we have.

i left for fifteen years and came back and the only thing that changed was that the pharmacy moved one block. the same people work at the same places. the same songs play at the same bars. the same kids are now teenagers. i don't know if this is comforting or terrifying. it might be both. it might be the same thing.

found a leather jacket today for fourteen dollars. it fits like it was made for me. there's a name written inside the collar in faded ink. it just says terrence. i don't know who terrence is. i don't know what happened to him. but i'm wearing his jacket now. i'm walking around in his life. that's the magic of thrifting. you become other people for ten dollars.

got a complete set of wedgwood teacups for nine dollars. someone's grandmother died. someone didn't want them. someone donated them. i am going to drink coffee out of these every morning for the rest of my life. i am going to hold the handles carefully. i am going to think about that grandmother. i am going to be grateful she existed.

the goodwill on cedar had a soviet army surplus coat for thirty dollars. i bought it. it's enormous on me. it smells like a basement. i love it more than i love most things in my life. i am going to wear it through every winter until i die. it is now my coat. it was someone else's coat for sixty years. now it's mine.

found a paperback at the bottom of a box. five cents. it was a copy of a book i loved when i was sixteen. but a different edition. with a different cover. i couldn't believe it. i bought it immediately. the bookseller said it was probably stolen from a library in 1978. she didn't care. i didn't care. some books just need to find you again.

estate sale today. a woman who collected ceramic animals. i mean collected. there were hundreds. they were arranged on every surface of her house. her children were selling them in batches. i bought a small ceramic owl for two dollars. the owl is sitting on my desk now. it is judging me. i hope the woman would be okay with this. i hope the owl is happy here.

the salvation army had a wedding dress for fifty dollars. it was beautiful. i don't need a wedding dress. i'm not getting married. i bought it anyway. i'm going to wear it in my apartment. i'm going to wear it while making dinner. i'm going to wear it because i can. wedding dresses are too beautiful to only wear once. that's not a thing i agreed to.

vintage cookbook from 1964. spiral bound. someone's handwritten notes in the margins. the previous owner liked her potatoes well-seasoned. she crossed out the salt amounts and wrote more more more in pencil. she also wrote her shopping list inside the back cover. flour, sugar, eggs, milk. it has been there for sixty years. i will not erase it. i will not.

found a desk for forty dollars. solid wood. probably oak. i'm not sure. one drawer sticks. one of the legs is wobbly. i don't care. i'm refinishing it this weekend. i will spend two hundred dollars on supplies to refinish a desk i bought for forty. this is the thrifting economy. this is the math. it makes no sense. i am not going to stop.

a friend gave me her grandmother's sewing machine. it weighs forty pounds. it is from 1952. it still works. it is olive green and gold and it has the original manual. i don't know how to sew. i'm going to learn. i'm going to make small bad things on this machine. i'm going to keep my friend's grandmother in my life by making bad pillowcases.

a box of photographs at a yard sale. fifty cents for the whole box. nobody i knew. nobody i'll ever know. but a wedding. a baby. a vacation. a christmas. dozens of small lives. i couldn't leave them in a box at a yard sale. i bought them. they're in my closet now. i don't know what to do with them. but they're not nothing. they're not nothing.

i never thought i'd write a love letter to anyone. i thought love letters were a thing other people did. people from old movies. straight people. but you sat on my porch last summer eating a peach and i thought oh. so this is what they were writing about. so this is what the songs were trying to say. so this is the whole entire thing.

the first time we held hands in public i was twenty-six and i had never done it before. i had never been able to. and you didn't make a big deal of it. you just took my hand at the farmer's market like you'd been doing it your whole life. and i wanted to cry but i didn't. i smiled at the tomatoes instead. i held your hand. and we kept walking.

i love that you laugh at your own jokes before you finish them. i love that you cry at sports movies. i love that you bring me coffee on saturdays before i'm awake and leave it on the bedside table where it gets cold. i love that you do that even though i never drink it cold. you keep trying. you keep loving me your way.

the night we met you said something nobody had ever said to me before. you said i think you're the most yourself when you're tired. and i thought about that for a year. and then i thought about it for another year. and now i'm thinking about it on the anniversary of the night we met. and i still don't know what you meant. and i still believe you.

we walked through the cemetery on our second date because it was the only place open after midnight. you pointed at a gravestone that said beloved wife and you said i want one of those. and i laughed. and you said no i mean it. i want to be someone's beloved wife. and i wanted to say me. me. let me. but i didn't. it was too soon. it's not too soon now.

i love the way you take up space. i grew up taught to make myself small. you grew up taught to make yourself big. and somehow we fit. somehow you take up exactly the space i was never allowed to take. and i don't have to anymore. you do it for both of us. and i can rest in your shadow when i need to. and you don't mind.

you wear my t-shirts to sleep in. they're too big on you. i could buy you t-shirts. you would wear them. but you wear mine and i don't know why and i don't want to ask because the answer might break the spell. you smell like me in the morning. that's the best gift i've ever been given. you smell like me. i smell like you. we are doing this. we are.

i wasted so much of my life thinking love wasn't for me. thinking i'd missed the window. thinking the kind of life people have together was a country i'd been denied a passport to. and then you. and then you. and i live there now. in that country. with you. and i'm not going back. i refuse to go back. they can't make me.

thank you for not making me explain anything. thank you for understanding the silence around my parents. thank you for never asking why i flinch sometimes when people walk too close on the sidewalk. thank you for holding my hand anyway in those moments. for being the response to every reflex i still have that was trained into me when i was small.

i was at the grocery store today and the woman in front of me was buying flowers and i thought i should buy flowers. for no reason. for the same reason every flower has ever been bought. so i did. they're on the kitchen table now. they're yellow. you'll come home and you'll be confused. and then you'll smile. and that's why. that's the whole answer.

the cafe i work at has a window seat that nobody seems to know about. it faces an alley but the morning sun comes down at exactly 10am and lights everything up gold. i sit there for an hour every day i'm there. i pretend i'm working. i'm not really working. i'm just sitting in the light. i'm just letting the day begin.

the espresso machine sounds like a small train. the milk steamer sounds like a small storm. the grinder sounds like a small earthquake. all day. all day. and somehow it's calming. somehow it's the soundtrack i've come to need to think. i can't write at home anymore. i need this. i need this specific noise.

the regulars at the cafe on grand are: the writer with the typewriter. the elderly couple who reads the paper together. the young woman who studies medical school flashcards. the dog who isn't allowed in but always comes in. the man who reads russian novels in russian. me. we don't talk. we nod. that's enough. that's everything.

the new cafe opened on third street and i don't know how to feel about it. it's beautiful. the chairs are real wood. the cups are real ceramic. but it's expensive. and it's busy. and the old cafe one block away is going to close because of it. and i don't know which one i should go to. i think i have to choose. i think this is a moral question.

i had a meeting with a stranger at a cafe today. she was an old friend of a friend. we sat across a small table and drank coffee and talked for three hours about everything. about her divorce. about my dead father. about the books we'd been reading. we walked out into the rain. we hugged. we'll probably never see each other again. and that was the whole point.

the worst sound in the world is the sound of someone packing up to leave a cafe table while you're waiting for one. you stand there pretending not to watch. you sip your coffee that's already cold. you wait. and you wait. and they're so slow. they have all the time in the world. and you have a deadline. and they don't know. and you don't say anything.

the barista at the place i go to wrote my name wrong on the cup for three years. i never corrected her. she wrote elizabeth instead of elise. one day she got it right. and i was a little sad. and i didn't know why. and i think i was attached to the misnaming. i think the misnaming was a kind of intimacy. it doesn't have to make sense.

found a cafe in a city i was visiting. it had two tables. it had a cat. it had a small bookshelf of paperbacks for trade. the man who ran it gave me the coffee for free because i looked like his daughter. he had not seen her in eleven years. he showed me her picture. she did not look like me. i drank the coffee. i hugged him. i left.

i wrote my book at a cafe over the course of three years. they let me sit there for hours and only buy one drink. they put a sign on the table eventually that said reserved for the writer. i didn't ask for the sign. it just appeared. i still don't know who put it there. i finished the book. they're in the acknowledgments. they don't know.

the cafe closed last week. they had been losing money for two years. the landlord wouldn't lower the rent. the owners cried at the going-away party. i cried too. so did everyone. it was just a cafe. it was also not just a cafe. it was where my whole adult life happened. i don't know where i'll go now. i don't know who i'll be.

the summer i was thirteen i went to a camp on a lake and i fell in love with a girl named magdalena who could not pronounce my name. she called me by the wrong name for two weeks. i let her. when i went home i wrote her one letter and she never wrote back. she lives in poland now. she's a doctor. i looked her up. i didn't reach out.

we built a raft one summer. it didn't work. it sank as soon as we got on it. we were eleven. we were furious. we worked on it for two weeks. the counselors had warned us. we didn't listen. and yet that summer is the summer i remember. the raft is the most important thing i remember from being eleven. you have to fail at something to remember it.

the camp had a chapel that nobody used except us. we'd sneak in at night and sit in the pews and tell each other secrets. i told them about my parents. they told me theirs. we were twelve. we didn't know how good we had it. we didn't know we'd never be that honest again. we thought everyone was like this. we thought this was just life.

my best friend at camp was a girl named bea who had asthma and the meanest sense of humor i've ever encountered in a child. she made me laugh until i couldn't breathe. she got sent home early one summer because she set off the fire alarm to get out of an archery competition. i didn't see her for ten years after that. then we ran into each other in chicago. we picked up exactly where we left off.

we sang the same song every campfire for ten years. i still remember every word. i could sing it tomorrow. i sang it in the shower last week. my partner asked what i was singing and i couldn't explain. she wouldn't get it. you have to have been there. you have to have been a kid on a wooden bench in front of a fire in the woods. otherwise it's just a song.

the camp shower house had no hot water. you got used to it. you had to. by week two it didn't even feel cold. by week three it felt good. i miss that. i miss the simplicity of an unheated shower. i miss not having choices. i miss when the only decision in a day was whether to swim before lunch or after. let me go back. let me be eleven.

the lake had an island in the middle. you weren't allowed to swim to it. we did anyway. the older kids dared us. we made it halfway and got scared and turned back. but for a moment in the middle of the lake i was alone in deeper water than i'd ever been in and i thought about how easy it would be to just keep going. then i didn't. i turned around. i grew up.

i kissed a boy named julian in the boat shed during a thunderstorm when i was fourteen. it was my first kiss. it was his first kiss too. we both pretended it wasn't. we both pretended we'd done this before. we hadn't. we knew the other was lying. it didn't matter. it was perfect anyway. it was the truest first kiss anyone has ever had.
