the food was terrible. everyone says this about camp food. but ours was specifically terrible. the spaghetti was somehow both undercooked and overcooked at the same time. the bread was always slightly stale. and yet i would eat that food right now if you put it in front of me. nostalgia makes everything edible. nostalgia is the strongest seasoning there is.

the last night of camp every summer we lit a bonfire and everyone read a letter they had written to themselves at the start of the session. the letters were small. they were not profound. they were what an eleven-year-old or twelve-year-old or thirteen-year-old thought was important. and then we threw them into the fire. and the fire took them. and we cried. all of us. every year.

we live in different time zones now but we keep a shared notes app where we write to each other when we think of something. she lives in melbourne. i live in chicago. we write little messages. a song. a recipe. a stupid thought. a bird we saw. we read them when we wake up. it's slower than texting. it's more like a letter. it's better.

i haven't seen her in person in four years. we still talk every week. we have a phone call every sunday. it's been on her calendar since 2019. it's never been cancelled. once she took the call from a hospital waiting room. once i took it from a train. once we both fell asleep on the call. it doesn't matter. we show up. that's the whole thing.

she sent me a package this week. it took six weeks to arrive. inside were three books, a postcard, a packet of tea from her local market, and a small rock she said i would understand. i don't understand. she has not explained. i am writing her back to ask. i am also leaving the rock where she sent it. it lives on my desk now. it watches me.

we used to live in the same apartment when we were twenty-two. we ate every meal together. we slept on the same fold-out couch some nights when one of us was sad. and now she's in another country and we go months without talking and we pick it up again like nothing happened. that's the kind of friendship that survives oceans. that's the kind of friendship you don't realize you have until you're tested by distance.

her grandmother died last week. she called me at 3am her time because i was the only person awake. we talked for two hours. she cried. i didn't know what to say. i didn't have to say anything. she just needed someone on the line. i made tea while she talked. she could hear the kettle. she said it was comforting. it was the most useful i've been in a year.

we wrote each other letters all through college. real letters. with stamps. it was the late 2000s. we could have texted. we didn't. we wrote letters. i still have all of hers. they're in a shoebox. she has all of mine. i hope. i don't know. i should ask. but maybe i don't want to know. maybe i want to imagine she has them.

she's coming to visit next month. we haven't seen each other in two years. i am cleaning the apartment. i am buying her favorite snacks. i am making a list of all the places i want to take her. i am also slightly nervous. what if we're different now. what if we don't fit anymore. and then i remember. it doesn't work that way. it never has. we always fit.

we have a running joke that started in 2014 and we are still doing the joke and neither of us remembers exactly how it started. we just keep doing it. it's not even funny anymore. it's just a thing. it's its own language. it's a small bridge across years. and it works. and it keeps working. it will probably outlive both of us.

she got married last summer and i couldn't go. i was sick. i hate that i couldn't go. she said it was okay. she sent me pictures. i cried looking at them. she looked so beautiful. her wife looked so happy. and i felt very far away. and i thought about the night i met her in 2008. and i thought about how much i love her. how much i still do.

long distance friendship is the slowest friendship. it gets less and asks for less. you can't share a meal. you can't drive someone to the airport. you can't sit in their kitchen at midnight. but somehow it survives. somehow it grows underground while you aren't looking. and when you see each other again it's all there. it's all still there. nothing was lost.

the rain started around eleven this morning and hasn't stopped. the cat is mad about it. she keeps going to the door and looking outside and turning around in disgust. she does this every hour like she's expecting the weather to have changed. it has not. it is not going to. but i admire her persistence. i admire her refusal to accept the world as it is.

all my plans for today are cancelled by rain and i feel a kind of relief i'm not sure i'm allowed to feel. i wanted to do those things. i committed to those things. but the rain decided for me. and now i can stay home and not feel guilty. the rain is permission. the rain is a small kind hand on my shoulder saying you can stay in.

i'm thinking about my grandmother who loved rain more than anyone i've ever known. she would open all the windows. she would sit by them and read. she said the smell of rain was her favorite smell. she said it smelled like beginnings. she was right. it does smell like beginnings. i never told her i thought she was right. she died nine years ago.

the city is quieter in the rain. the streets emptier. the people more wrapped up. i went for a walk under the umbrella my dad gave me ten years ago. it's losing one of the spokes. i should replace it. i won't. i'll keep walking under it until it falls apart. there are some objects you have to use until they're done. there are some objects that are a promise.

rainy day depression is real and so is rainy day joy and i can't always tell which one i'm in. today is one of the joy ones. i don't know what made it different. i'm sitting by the window with hot chocolate and reading and the dog is asleep at my feet and i feel like a soft animal in a soft world. it's not always like this. i'm going to enjoy it.

we lost power at 3pm and didn't get it back until 8. for five hours we sat in the dim apartment and i lit every candle we own and we made sandwiches in the not-quite-dark and we played cards with a deck that was missing the four of clubs. we used a piece of paper instead. it was one of the best afternoons i can remember. the rain made all of it possible.

the gutters are clogged. i can hear the water spilling over the side of the roof onto the brick. it sounds like a waterfall. it is also a small disaster. i should clean the gutters. i won't. that's a problem for spring. for now i am going to enjoy the waterfall sound. for now i am going to pretend the roof is a wonder of nature and not a maintenance crisis.

my mother always made stew on rainy days. i don't know why. it wasn't a rule. it just happened. and now whenever it rains i want stew. i don't even like stew that much. but i make it. and i eat it. and i think about her. and the apartment smells like her. and she is alive in some small way for an evening. food is a kind of seance.

i used to hate rain. i grew up somewhere it rained all the time. i wanted sun. i moved south. i got sun. and then i missed the rain. and now i live somewhere it rains again and i love it. i wasted years complaining about something that turned out to be one of my favorite things. i wonder how many other things i'm doing that to right now.

the rain stopped just as the sun was going down. the streets are shining. the sky is pink and orange. the air smells like wet pavement and lilacs. i opened the door and stood there for a few minutes. nobody else was outside. it was like the city had been washed and put back. it was like the day was making a small apology. i accepted it. i went inside.

this book has an inscription. to charlotte, with all my love, from your father. christmas 1962. i don't know who charlotte was. i don't know what she did with this book. but it ended up in a used bookstore in a different state forty years later. and now it's mine. and i'm thinking about her father. and about her. and about love that lasts longer than people.

my favorite paperback has been water-damaged. i found it that way. someone had spilled tea on it years before i bought it. you can see the ring on the cover. and the pages are warped in the middle. and yet i love this copy more than any pristine copy would be. the damage is the history. the damage is what makes it mine.

i collect used copies of one specific novel. i have eleven of them. each one is different. different cover. different edition. different markings. i don't know why i do this. i don't reread it. they live on a shelf. they are a kind of monument to one book. a small library of one. someone will inherit this and not know what to do with it. i'm okay with that.

the bookstore on third has a cat who sleeps in the philosophy section. i go in just to visit the cat. i pick up a book. i pet the cat. i put the book back. i leave. i have done this for three years. i have never bought a book there. i feel guilty about it. last week i finally bought one. it was a children's book about a cat. she would have liked it.

found a used poetry collection that had a pressed flower between pages 47 and 48. it was a violet. it was so old it was the color of a bruise. i put it back exactly where i found it. i bought the book. now the violet lives between pages 47 and 48 in my apartment. i think about her. whoever pressed it. whatever she was reading. why she chose those pages.

my favorite kind of used book is one that has been read. one whose spine is cracked. whose pages are dog-eared. whose margins have notes. i don't trust a used book that looks unread. it was sitting on a shelf for a reason. it didn't earn anyone's love. i want the loved ones. the loved ones love you back somehow. i can't explain it. they just do.

the woman who runs the bookstore down the street has a face like an old painting. she's been there forty years. she remembers what every regular reads. she pulled a book off the shelf for me last week before i'd even said what i was looking for. she said i think you're ready for this one. i was. i don't know how she knew. she is in the business of knowing.

i found a copy of a book i was reading at the exact same time as someone else. i could see her notes in the margins. she had underlined the same lines i had been underlining. she had drawn the same small stars next to the same paragraphs. i don't know who she is. but we read this book together. across time. across her copy and mine. i wish i could find her.

the box of free books at the curb. i can't walk past it. it doesn't matter what i have to do. i have to look. half the time the books are bad. half the time i don't take any. but i have to look. it's a compulsion. it might be a love language. the books are saying take me. take me. and how am i supposed to walk past.

this book costs three dollars. i can afford it. i can afford ten of these books. and yet every time i pay for a used book i feel a small thrill. like i got away with something. like the book and i conspired together against the world. like there's a secret economy of people who know the value of these things. and we are not telling.

the dress i bought last weekend was made in 1968. that's older than my mother. i'm wearing the same dress that a stranger wore to a party fifty-six years ago. she doesn't know that. she might be dead. she might be ninety years old somewhere. the dress remembers her better than any of us can remember anything. that's the thing about vintage. it remembers.

found a wool coat from the 1940s with the original buttons. the label is from a department store that closed in 1972. the inside is monogrammed. someone named e.r. owned this. it fits me like it was made for me. and maybe in a sense it was. e.r. was probably my size. e.r. had probably my taste. e.r. and i are sharing a coat across eighty years.

my favorite thing about vintage is the construction. the seams. the linings. the way buttons are sewn on. nothing falls apart. nothing pills. the clothes are made to be inherited. they are made to last longer than any one person. fast fashion is a recent crime. for most of history people made things to last. we forgot. we'll have to remember.

the silk slip i found at the estate sale was the color of bruised peaches. it was hand-sewn. it had been mended carefully in one spot by someone who knew what they were doing. i bought it for six dollars. i feel guilty about that. it should have cost more. the woman who owned it would be sad. i hope wherever she is she knows i'm taking care of it.

the rule with vintage is that if it fits you have to buy it. you can't think about it. you can't sleep on it. you can't come back tomorrow. if it fits and you love it you buy it now. that's the rule. that's the only rule. people who don't follow this rule end up with regrets that last decades. i have those regrets. i learned. i am better now.

i wear my grandmother's wedding ring on my middle finger. she gave it to me before she died. she said i don't want it to go into a drawer. wear it. so i wear it. it's a thin gold band. nothing fancy. but it has been on a hand for sixty-seven years. it knows things. it is more myself than most of my own clothes.

the velvet blazer was made in italy in 1979. i bought it in a thrift store in vermont in 2018. i wore it to my book launch in 2022. someone in the audience came up after and said her mother had owned the same blazer. i showed her the label. she started crying. her mother is dead now. i offered to give her the blazer. she said no. she said you wear it. you're keeping her alive.

i wear vintage every day. people ask me why. the honest answer is that new clothes don't fit my body. they are made for a body i don't have. vintage was made when there were more body types. when sewing was custom. when nothing was meant to be one size fits all. vintage fits me because it was made before fits were mass produced. that's the secret.

the apron my mother gave me was hand-embroidered by her aunt in poland in 1958. it has a small red flower in the corner. the embroidery is uneven in places. you can see where she made mistakes and corrected them. i wear this apron when i cook. i think about her hands. i think about how they made this for someone she loved. i never met her. but the apron knew her.

i bought a pair of boots from the 1970s. they were heavily resoled. they had been worn for decades. they were a wreck. i had them restored by a cobbler who said he hadn't worked on boots like these in twenty years. he charged me too much. i didn't care. those boots have been my boots for two years now. they have outlived three pairs of new boots i bought after them.

i found a stack of letters my grandmother wrote to my grandfather during the war. they are in her looping handwriting. they are addressed to him at a base in france. they smell faintly of an attic. she is asking him to come home. she is asking gently. she is asking like a woman who knows she has to wait. i can't read them all at once. i can only read one a day.

i wrote a letter to my best friend yesterday and put it in the mail today. she lives twenty minutes away. we could see each other anytime. but i wanted her to get something in her mailbox that wasn't a bill. i wanted her to know i was thinking about her at the kitchen table. with a pen. for forty minutes. that's a different kind of love.

the box of pen pal letters from middle school is still under my bed. i don't reread them. i don't open the box. but i know it's there. i know that another twelve-year-old in mexico used to write to me about her dog. and i used to write back about mine. and we kept it up for three years. and i don't know what happened to her. but i hope she's okay.

the postcard collection in my desk drawer is from people i barely know. a coworker who went to japan. a friend's mother who travels constantly. a cousin who lives in argentina. they are not for me really. they are just postcards. and yet i keep them. i keep all of them. they are evidence that i was thought of when someone was far away. that's not nothing.

the last letter my father wrote me was on the back of a receipt. it was four sentences. he wasn't a long-letter person. it said i'm proud of you. you're doing well. don't worry about me. i love you. he died eight months later. i keep the receipt in my wallet. i have not transferred it to a frame. i don't want to make it precious. i want it to stay everyday.

i still buy stamps in person at the post office. the clerk knows me. she keeps the good ones aside. last week she gave me a set with old paintings on them. i used one to mail a card to my mother. my mother called me to say she loved the stamp. she didn't mention what i wrote in the card. she just talked about the stamp. that's love. that's love too.

writing a letter is a kind of meditation. you sit down. you choose a pen. you put paper in front of you. you think about the person. you write to them slowly. you can't take it back. you can't delete. you have to mean what you say. you have to be patient with yourself. you have to let it be imperfect. it's the opposite of an email. it's the opposite of a text.

i kept the letters i wrote in college but never sent. some were love letters. some were apology letters. some were letters to my parents about things i couldn't say out loud. i found them last week cleaning out a box. i was twenty-two when i wrote them. i'm thirty-eight now. i recognized myself. i also didn't. i didn't send them. but i'm glad i wrote them.

my friend's daughter is six years old and she has started writing me letters. they are mostly drawings. they are mostly addressed to madam dear lady which is what she thinks adults call each other. i write back. i match her seriousness. i match her formality. i sign mine sincerely. she sends them in envelopes she decorated herself. i keep every one. i'm raising her too in a small way.

if i die before my mother, the only thing i would want her to read is a letter i wrote her last december and never sent. it's in my desk. it says everything. it apologizes for things she doesn't know she's owed an apology for. it thanks her for things she doesn't know she gave me. i hope she reads it. or i hope i tell her instead. one of the two. preferably both.

the dog is six pounds and thinks she is a tiger. she barks at delivery trucks. she barks at deer. she barks at the wind sometimes if it carries something interesting on it. she does not know she is six pounds. and i will not tell her. she is doing important work. she is keeping us safe from threats. some of those threats are imagined. but the energy is real.

we went on a hike. the dog rode in my backpack for most of it. her legs are short. the trail was long. she was not embarrassed. she rode like a queen. she pointed her face into the wind. she was the only dog in the backpack. all other dogs walked. we got compliments. we stopped for photos. she enjoyed every minute of it.

the dog has discovered that she can climb onto the kitchen counter via the cat tree we got for the cat. she did this once. now she does it constantly. there is no food on the counter she cares about. she just wants to be up there. she just wants to see things from above. she just wants to look out the window from a new angle. i can't blame her. i don't.

her name is olive. she has been my dog for four years. i adopted her when she was three. she has lived more life than i have, probably. she came with a name and i didn't change it. she came with a sweater i still let her wear. she came with a small piece of fabric from her previous home. she sleeps with it. i'm not allowed to wash it. i wouldn't dare.

took the dog to the vet today. she was furious. she was betrayed. she gave me the look. the one that says i thought we were friends. and now we are leaving the vet and i have given her three treats and one piece of chicken and she still has not forgiven me. small dogs have long memories. she will hold this against me for at least another twenty-four hours.

she has a best friend at the dog park. a great dane named huckleberry. they are absurd together. she is half his head. they roll around. they chase each other. he is very gentle with her. she is not very gentle with him. their owners are also friends now because of them. i never met him before huck. i go to coffee with him every saturday now. small dogs make big lives.

olive came in from the yard with a small piece of mulch in her mouth and would not let me take it from her. she carried it around the apartment for three hours. she put it in her bed at one point. she took it back out. she licked it. she napped near it. i don't know what the mulch represented to her. but to her it was clearly the most important thing in her week.

she snores like an old man. i could record her. people wouldn't believe a six-pound dog was making those sounds. she snores so loudly i can hear her from the next room. she snores so loudly the cat sometimes leaves the bedroom to escape it. she is not embarrassed. she should be. she does not have shame. she is a small dog with the sleep habits of a retired sea captain.

she has a small wardrobe. five sweaters. two raincoats. a halloween costume i bought as a joke. she wears them all. she likes the orange one best. when i pull it out she does a small dance. she does not do a dance for any of the other sweaters. the orange one is special. i don't know what makes it special. she does. i defer to her judgment.

people stop us on the street to comment on her size. she is used to it. i am used to it. it has stopped being a conversation. i just say yes she is small. yes she is fully grown. yes she is six pounds. and they say oh my god how cute. and they reach for her. and she lets them. she is the ambassador of small dogs everywhere. she is a small dog professional. she is the boss.

the group meets every wednesday in the back room of the library. we have been meeting for six years. there are eight of us. two of us have died. we have not replaced them. their chairs are still there. nobody sits in them. we just leave them. we knit. we talk. we say their names sometimes. ann would have loved this yarn. judith hated this pattern. they are still with us. they are still in the room.

i learned to knit when i was eleven. my grandmother taught me. she said this skill is a kind of currency. she said you can always make a gift. you can always make something to keep warm. she was right. i have never been without a project. i have been knitting for thirty-six years. i have made hundreds of things. i think about her every time i cast on.

we are knitting hats for the hospital this month. for the nicu. for the babies who come early. tiny hats. so small they fit on my fist. we have made forty-three so far. we want to make a hundred. we will probably make more. we are old women with time on our hands. our hands are useful. that is the point. our hands are still useful.

there's a woman in the group who doesn't actually knit. she just comes for the conversation. she crochets. we tease her about it. she takes it well. she is the youngest of us. she is sixty-four. she calls us the elders. she is not wrong. we are. we are. we welcome her anyway. crocheters are also welcome here. we are not gatekeepers.

i made a sweater last winter that took me four months. it is the best thing i have ever made. it is also slightly too big in the shoulders. i wear it anyway. i wear it almost every day in the winter. people compliment it. i tell them i made it. they are surprised. they shouldn't be. women have been making their own clothes since the beginning of clothes.

the yarn store on belmont is run by a woman named patricia who is intimidating in the way old librarians are intimidating. she will judge your project. she will tell you the yarn is wrong. she will redirect you. she is always correct. i have learned to listen. i have made better things since listening. she has saved me from a number of disasters. i love her. she terrifies me. i love her.

i taught my granddaughter to knit when she was nine. she is now sixteen. she still knits sometimes. mostly she texts. but she knits. she made a scarf last christmas and gave it to me. it was a little uneven. it was beautiful. she thanked me for teaching her. i didn't know what to say. i hugged her. that's how the knowledge moves. from hands to hands. across decades. across lives.

i ripped out the whole sweater last night. all eight inches of it. the pattern was wrong. i had been doing it wrong for a week. i didn't want to know. i finally let myself know. and then i ripped it back to the cast-on. and i cried a little. and then i started again. and the new version is better. you have to be willing to undo. that's the lesson. that's the lesson.

the sound of eight pairs of needles working at once is the most peaceful sound i know. it's not silent. but it's not loud. it's a kind of soft rhythm. it's a small forest of small clicks. it's a hundred years of women doing this together. it's a sound that goes back further than the lightbulb. and we are still doing it. and that's a kind of magic.

marjorie brought scones today. she does this once a month. they are slightly burned on the bottom. we eat them anyway. we tell her they are perfect. she pretends to believe us. nobody actually believes us. but we all play the game. that's part of the knitting circle. we lie about the scones. we tell the truth about everything else. it balances out.

the fridge hums in that specific way it does at 2am, like it's keeping a secret. i'm eating cold spaghetti from the container with a fork that's slightly too big for the job. there's something about kitchens at this hour that feels like a different country. the tile is colder. the light from the open fridge does that yellow thing. my mother used to do this exact thing, i remember now, watching her shadow on the wall when i couldn't sleep as a kid. i guess we both ended up here.

boiling water is meditation if you let it be. you stand there. you watch it not happen. you watch it not happen some more. and then suddenly the surface breaks and everything is steam and bubbles and there's no in-between moment you can point to where it changed. life is mostly like that i think. you're just standing there one day and then you're not.

made toast at midnight which i think is a love letter to yourself sometimes. butter melting into the holes. honey on top. ate it standing up over the sink so the crumbs would go somewhere acceptable. the cat watched me with that judgmental look she has but i think secretly she approves of small acts of self-care even when they look stupid.

found a single mug at the back of the cupboard that says world's okayest dad which is wild because no one in this apartment is anyone's dad. previous tenant artifact. archeology of strangers. i'm using it now for tea and feeling weird allegiance to a man i've never met who was either being self-deprecating or had a really mean kid.

there's a moth in the cupboard. she's been there three days. i've named her gretchen and i am not going to kill her because at this point we have a relationship. every time i open the door to get the cereal she does her dramatic flutter and i say hi gretchen and she pretends not to know me. companionable.

i think the most honest hour is the one where you stand in front of an open fridge with no real plan, just vibes, just hoping something inside will tell you who you are tonight. usually it's hummus. sometimes it's pickles. once it was a slice of cake i forgot existed and i ate it standing up and that was a religious experience honestly.

tea at 1am for no reason, just because the kettle was right there and i wanted to hold something warm. didn't even want to drink it really. just wanted the ritual. the scoop, the pour, the steam. i think a lot of life is making excuses to do small slow things that you don't strictly need to do.

do you ever stand in your kitchen and just feel like a ghost? not in a bad way. just like you're observing the room from a slight remove. the apples in the bowl. the calendar on the wall still on february. the dish rack that needs to be emptied. all of it just continuing without your input. peaceful.

tried to make a grilled cheese at 3am and burned it on both sides while leaving the middle cold. ate it anyway. it was the worst grilled cheese in recorded history. i loved her. i thanked her for her service. she will be remembered.

the kitchen at night is full of small mechanical sounds that you don't notice during the day. the click of the heater. the soft tick of the clock. the gurgle the pipes make. it's like the apartment is whispering to itself and you're just allowed to listen for a little while.

watching towns go by from a bus window is one of the better drugs. you don't know anyone, no one knows you, you're a streak passing through. there's a guy mowing his lawn and he doesn't know you exist and you'll never see him again and somehow that's beautiful instead of sad.

the woman across the aisle is eating an entire rotisserie chicken with her bare hands and i have never respected anyone more in my life. she has a plastic bag for the bones. she has wet wipes. she has prepared. this is a woman who knows what a six hour bus ride requires.

i tried to read on the bus but the road is too bumpy and my brain feels like it's sloshing. so now i'm just looking out the window and listening to the same three songs and feeling like the main character of a movie no one will ever make.

there's a baby behind me who has been screaming for forty minutes and the dad keeps apologizing to everyone and i keep saying it's okay even though it's not really okay, but it's also not the baby's fault, and it's not the dad's fault, and somehow this collective suffering is a kind of intimacy.

we stopped at a gas station in the middle of nowhere and i got out and the air smelled like diesel and pine trees and something distinctly midwestern that i can't name. i bought a bag of chips and a coke and got back on the bus and felt like i had touched something real.

the man in front of me has been watching the same youtube video on full volume without headphones for two hours. it's something about lawnmowers. i could describe to you in detail the difference between a john deere x350 and a x370 even though i would not be able to point to a lawn if my life depended on it.

i think the best part of a bus ride is when it's almost dark and the inside of the bus is dim and everyone is in their own little world with their headphones and their phones, and outside the world is doing its slow blue thing, and you feel like you're suspended between places.

fell asleep with my head against the window and woke up with a circular bruise on my forehead from the seal of the glass. there are now small towns i have passed through entirely in my sleep, places that exist for me only as the brief sensation of slowing down and speeding up again, ghost-towns in the truest sense.

everyone on this bus is going somewhere with a whole life i'll never know about. the woman with the laminated bible. the kid with the skateboard. the older guy who keeps making phone calls in a language i can't place. we're a temporary collective. we'll never assemble like this again.

the bus driver has a small fan clipped to the dashboard and a photo taped next to the speedometer of what i assume is his granddaughter. he hummed for about a hundred miles. i don't think he knew he was doing it. it was lovely.

started a new sampler tonight. just basic running stitch in this dusty pink dmc that i've been hoarding for like two years waiting for the right project. there's something so satisfying about the rhythm of it. needle up, needle down. the fabric pulled taut in the hoop. my cat watching like she might pounce but she never does, she's mostly given up on the embroidery floss as prey.

finally finished the mushroom piece i've been working on since february. french knots for the spores on the underside of the cap. it took forever. my eyes hurt. but here she is, in all her glory, a tiny chanterelle on a square of linen, slightly off-center because i miscounted my threads at the start and refused to start over.

the back of my embroidery looks like a crime scene and the front looks like a polite garden and i think that's the most accurate metaphor for being a person that i've ever made by accident. presenting one side, hiding the chaos of the construction.

ordered new floss from a small shop on etsy run by a woman named brenda who included a handwritten note that said 'happy stitching xx'. brenda i don't know you but i would die for you. the colors are gorgeous. she dyes them herself in her kitchen which i find deeply correct.

tried satin stitch for the first time and listen. listen. satin stitch is hard. mine looks like the threads got into a fight on the way to the fabric. i'm calling it a learning experience but really it's a small disaster on a 4 inch hoop and i'm going to leave it on the wall to humble myself.

found my grandmother's old embroidery scissors in a box of stuff my mom sent me. tiny stork-shaped ones, the beak is where you cut. they're still sharper than anything i own. i've been holding them all afternoon thinking about her hands. i don't even remember if she embroidered, but she had these.

current wip: a tiny bowl of cherries on a piece of natural linen. they're going to be ridiculous and i love them already. i'm using six strands of red because i want them to look like cartoon cherries and not real cherries. art lies. that's the whole point.

had a whole stitch-along with a friend on a video call tonight and we both got nothing done because we just talked the whole time but the embroidery was sort of the excuse for talking and i think that's the point of any craft circle in any era anywhere.

thinking about how every stitch is a decision. when to come up, when to go down. it's basically just choosing a million times in a row. some days that's exhausting and some days that's the most calming thing in the world.

for the love of everything please learn from my mistakes and do use a hoop frame for anything larger than four inches. my hands are cramping. my neck is cramping. i am one with the linen. i have become the embroidery. send help and also more dmc 310.

third week on the boat and i've stopped noticing the gentle rocking which i'm told means i've finally adjusted. now when i visit a friend's apartment i feel weirdly seasick on dry land. the brain is a wonderful idiot. it'll learn anything you teach it and then act like it always knew.

made coffee on the boat this morning while the marina was still asleep. herons stalking in the shallows. the slap of water against the hull. a fog low on the surface. i thought how absurd it is that some people have to drive to find a view like this, and i just have to open my eyes.

had to fix the bilge pump today and i have learned more about my own boat in three hours than i did in three months of living on her. i am covered in something that smells like diesel and lake water and i would not trade it. when you live on a boat you are her entire medical team.

neighbor on b-dock brought over half a smoked salmon he caught yesterday and i gave him a bottle of wine and we sat on the deck for an hour talking about nothing while the sun went down. there's something about boat people. you exchange. you barter. you participate.

storm came through last night and i sat in the cabin with all the lights off just listening to it. rain like fistfuls of marbles on the roof. the boat creaking and shifting on her lines. i felt safer than i have ever felt in any apartment. she's a good little boat. she's holding.

the bathroom is the size of a phone booth and the shower is the bathroom. once you accept that this is fine, your standards for what constitutes a bathroom expand into a kind of zen koan. yes the toilet is also kind of the sink. yes the floor is also kind of the shower drain. it all works out.

you don't appreciate fresh water until you live somewhere where it's finite. every time i fill the tank i think about the rivers it came from. every time i wash dishes i'm in a small negotiation. it has made me much better, i think, in ways i didn't expect.

got a tiny basil plant for the galley window and now my entire life is about this basil plant. is she getting enough sun. is she too close to the porthole. did the salt air get her. she's thriving actually. i think she likes it here. we both do.

fell asleep with the porthole open and woke up to a curious mallard on the deck looking in at me like he was checking my work. i don't know what i did wrong but he seemed disappointed. he left without saying anything. i'm still thinking about him.

the marina office has a free books cart and i have read more in three months than i did in the previous three years. mostly thrillers. occasionally a tide chart. once a self-help book i couldn't put down because the woman who donated it had written angry annotations in the margins, which were better than the book itself.

4am dough turn. the kitchen is warm from the proofers and the smell is somewhere between yeast and brown butter and i could stay in here forever. the radio plays softly so we don't wake the neighborhood, just sam and me and the rhythmic slap of dough on the marble counter, the world hasn't started yet, we're inventing it from flour.

the croissants didn't laminate right today and i could see it the moment i opened the dough. too warm in the kitchen yesterday. the butter melted in places it shouldn't have. we'll bake them anyway, they'll taste fine, but they won't have that flake. it's like a failed sentence you publish anyway because you have to.

first customer of the morning is always martha at 6:15 sharp for a sourdough boule and a pain au chocolat for her grandson. she pretends she doesn't see when i throw in an extra cookie. she's been doing this for three years. we have a system. it's a very quiet kind of love.

the dough has been ready since 3am, the levain bubbling under cling film. there's an art to knowing when a sourdough is alive enough to bake. you press it gently. it springs back like a cheek. she tells you what she needs and if you listen, she'll never lie to you.

burned my forearm on the oven rack pulling out a tray of palmiers and now there's a perfect stripe across the skin that i'll have for a week and that mary will roll her eyes at because i refuse to wear the long mitts she keeps buying for me. the badge of every baker who thought they could grab the tray just this once.

the bakery cat is named butter and she is unionized in the sense that she does whatever she wants. she lives in the back office, comes out for opening, accepts a small amount of cream from a saucer at 9am, and goes to bed at 11. she has more job security than any of us.

i think the best part of being a baker is that nobody knows what you've done by the time they walk through the door. they don't see the 4am turn or the temperatures or the proofing checks. they see bread. they see a glossy crust. they take it home and butter it. it's a very quiet kind of magic.

we made cardamom buns today as a special. by 11 they were gone. by noon people were standing at the window pointing and i had to come out and say sorry, no more, come earlier tomorrow. there was a small riot in the form of disappointed sighs. cardamom buns are a kind of currency in this neighborhood.

the new apprentice cried today over a tray of scones that came out flat and i remembered being 22 and standing exactly there. i told her about the time i scorched twelve loaves and slept under the prep table and woke up to my boss laughing at me. she laughed which is the entire point. you have to laugh at the bread eventually.

by the end of the day my apron is a topographic map of where i've been. a streak of jam from the danish. a smear of chocolate from the pain au. a dusting of flour everywhere as standard. i hang it on the hook and walk home through the morning rush, smelling like a cinnamon roll, smiling at everyone.

the sea today is the color of old denim, washed out where the light hits it. one tanker on the horizon moving so slowly it might as well not be moving. a gull doing nothing in particular. i've been here on this bench for an hour and i couldn't tell you what i've been thinking about, which i think is the whole point of sitting by the sea.

tide is coming in. you can hear it before you can see it. there's a specific sound when a wave catches a particular rock and it sounds exactly like a sigh, and i swear sometimes the sea is just out here sighing at us, doing its slow patient work.

a dog ran straight into the surf and his owner stood on the sand looking horrified. the dog came out fine. the dog was thrilled. the dog has discovered the secret of life. his owner doesn't know yet but i'm sure she'll figure it out eventually. the sea will not be denied if you have a dog.

i think the sea is the only thing i've ever truly felt small next to without it being a bad feeling. mountains make me feel small in a way that feels like a warning. the sea makes me feel small in a way that feels like an invitation.

found a sea glass in the tideline today, pale green, the color of old bottles. soft on every edge. it's been in the water for what, fifty years, eighty? something someone threw away long before i was born, polished smooth and given back to me. i don't believe in much but i believe in the sea making gifts.

the fishermen come out at dawn with their buckets and their lines and they don't talk to each other, they just nod, and they cast, and they stand there for hours. i envy the way they wait. they're not waiting impatiently. they're not even really waiting. they're just there. with the sea. doing the thing.

the gulls were doing that thing where they all turn at once and you wonder how they decided. some invisible vote. some signal you can't see. and they all wheeled south and then they all wheeled east and then they all landed on a single rock as if it was rehearsed. nature's choreography is criminally underappreciated.

salt in my hair. salt on my lips. salt on the bench i'm sitting on, somehow. the air here is doing a slow soft sanding of everything. nothing stays new by the sea. nothing pretends to. it's all just patina, all the way down.

stayed until the sun was almost down and the water turned to molten copper and then to mercury and then to something so dark it looked like ink. the lighthouse blinked on at exactly the moment it always does. there are still some things in the world you can set your watch by.

two kids were trying to build a sandcastle but the tide was working against them. they didn't seem to care. they kept building. one wall fell, they built another. the sea took it, they built it back. i thought, somewhere in this is the answer to a question i didn't know i was asking.

tonight at the corner cafe a girl in a yellow cardigan read a poem about her grandmother's hands and the entire room went so quiet you could hear the espresso machine three rooms back. she didn't look up once. she was reading it to her own shoes. but every single one of us was reading it with her.

my poem went over okay i think. there was a small polite ripple of finger snaps. one woman at the back tilted her head in that way that means she liked one specific line. i'll take it. that's everything. that's the whole reason to write poems at open mics, for one head-tilt from one stranger.

there's a guy who comes every wednesday and reads the same poem about his ex-wife and we all know it by heart now. we don't even mind. it's part of the architecture of this room. the poem is bad. the ritual is sacred. we snap politely. he sits back down. balance is restored.

shaking when i got up to the mic which is humiliating because i know everyone here, but the shaking is the price of admission and it never goes away no matter how many times you do it. i think people who don't shake aren't reading poems they care about.

the host tonight wore a denim jacket with a pin that said 'be gentle with yourself' and she introduced every poet like they were her family. when she said my name she looked right at me and i felt twenty feet tall. there are people who hold a room together. she's one of them.

someone read a poem about doing the dishes and i nearly cried which is embarrassing in public but the line was 'i scrubbed the pan he used to make me eggs in / and then i made eggs in it for myself' and what was i supposed to do, not cry?

the cafe owner makes a special drink on open mic nights called the bad metaphor and it's just a latte with extra cinnamon but every time we order one we feel like we're in on something. small joys. small inside jokes. you build a scene out of these things or you don't build one at all.

tonight a fifteen year old got up and read something about her dog dying and i swear half the room was openly crying. i was openly crying. she handled the mic like she'd been doing it for thirty years. some people are just born already old in the right way.

tried to memorize my poem and forgot the third stanza on stage and just stood there for what felt like a year. then i said 'so anyway' and laughed and read it off my phone and the audience laughed with me and it was, in a way, better than the polished version would have been.

the thing about open mics is that they're a tiny radical pocket of attention. for three minutes someone gets to be heard. no scrolling. no interrupting. just a room of strangers giving you their ears. it shouldn't feel revolutionary but it does, in this century, in this world, it does.

shot my last frame of pack 600 today on the fire escape with the morning light slanting through the railings and i watched it develop in my palm like an old photograph being born. the colors came up wrong, too pink, too warm, but i love her anyway, she's exactly what the morning felt like, which is maybe the only thing a polaroid is for.

the magic of an instant photo is also its curse. you only get one. you can't try again. there's no 'wait let me check the screen.' you commit. you press. you get whatever you get. and you have to love it because there's no other version of that moment, and there never will be.

got a polaroid of my friend laughing tonight that came out perfect, blue light, just the corner of her glasses catching the lamp, mouth wide open mid-cackle. these are the photos that get pinned to the fridge for a decade. these are the ones you'll look at when you're eighty.

the camera ate a pack of film today. i don't know why. she just refused to spit them out and when i opened the back to see what happened, i ruined the next two frames in the process. the polaroid is the only relationship in my life where i forgive this kind of behavior. it's part of the contract.

writing little notes on the white border under the photo with a fine-point pen so i don't forget. today at the diner. the second i knew. the cat in the window of the antique shop on 7th. these aren't captions, exactly. more like marginalia.

the dog won't stop moving when i try to take her picture so i have an entire wall of blurry shots of a brown blur that vaguely resembles a dog. they are all called 'pearl' and they are all my favorite photos i have ever taken. she is constantly in motion and the camera is constantly trying to keep up.

found an old polaroid in a book at a thrift store, a kid in front of a christmas tree, dated 1981 in pencil. no name. nothing else. someone's whole moment, abandoned. i took her home. i put her on my bookshelf. she lives here now. she gets to keep existing.

polaroids cost more per frame than they should and that's also the point. you slow down. you think before you press. there is no 'just one more.' every photo is a decision. every photo is a small bet that this thing in front of you is worth a piece of plastic film.

took a self-portrait in the bathroom mirror, flash bouncing off the glass into a bright white sun in the corner of the frame, and i think she came out perfect, the way a photo of yourself in your own bathroom is perfect. honest. unposed. a small accident of light.

my favorite thing is when a polaroid develops weird. an unexpected light leak. a streak of color that wasn't supposed to be there. some chemical mishap that made the photo more beautiful, not less. mistakes are often the better art. ask any old painter.

today is a soup day. couldn't get out of bed until 11, made it to the kitchen, sat in the sun on the floor for twenty minutes, made soup, ate half of it, went back to bed. that's the whole day. i'm trying to be gentle with myself about what counts as a day. it counts if i made soup. soup is a day.

the worst part of this isn't the tired, it's the not-knowing. is today a flare. is tomorrow. did i do too much yesterday. should i not do that walk. i used to plan in weeks and now i plan in hours and even that is sometimes ambitious. learning to live in the smaller unit.

found a little community online of people doing the same thing and it has saved my life i think. just the not-being-alone of it. just someone else saying yeah, that's the brain fog talking, yeah, the postural thing is real, yeah, you're not making this up. validation is medicine.

good day today. did a load of laundry. walked to the corner and back. read for twenty minutes without falling asleep. these things would have been nothing two years ago. now they are a triumph. i'm not being dramatic. they actually are. you have to recalibrate.

my best friend visited and we just lay on the couch watching old episodes of something we'd both already seen, and she made me a cup of tea, and we didn't really talk, and that was the best afternoon i've had in months. real love is somebody sitting quietly with you while you're depleted.

trying to be okay with the fact that i don't know who i'm going to be when this passes. or if. that's the hard one. or if. but every day i'm finding small versions of myself that didn't exist before either, the one who notices birds, the one who can be slow on purpose. she's not nothing.

the brain fog is the strangest part because it doesn't feel like anything, it just makes everything feel further away. like there's a pane of glass between me and the room. i'll be reading a sentence and realize i've been on it for five minutes. it's a kind of grief, this not-being-here.

pacing. pacing. pacing. the doctors keep saying it like a mantra. don't push through. stop before you have to stop. i used to be someone who finished things, who pushed through, who got tired in the middle and kept going. that person nearly killed me. learning to be the other person is its own job.

wrote a list today of things i'm grateful for and it was, in no order: a sunny window, ginger tea, my cat's foot pads, an audiobook with a soothing narrator, a single completed task. small list. real list. i'm not pretending. but the list exists, which is itself a kind of yes.

the rest is the work. for years i thought the work was the doing. now i know the rest is the work and the doing is the result of the work. it's a complete inversion of how i used to think about everything. uncomfortable. necessary. true.

the second floor of the library has a specific kind of silence that other silences don't have. it's not absence of sound, it's like the sound is being absorbed by all the paper. you can hear someone turn a page two tables over. you can hear the radiator settle. it's the closest i ever get to a held breath.

the librarian at the front desk has perfected the friendly-but-quiet voice and i would like to thank her, on behalf of everyone studying for finals, for the consistency of her welcomes. she is the soft on-ramp into this temple of paper.

the old man who naps in the periodicals every afternoon has the same routine. he picks up the new yorker. he reads about three lines. he falls asleep with the magazine on his chest. forty minutes later he wakes up, puts the magazine back on the rack, and leaves. it is the most beautiful daily practice.

found my favorite spot taken today by a teenager with headphones and a stack of math textbooks and i had to sit in the second-best spot which is by the window but next to the stairs which means people walk by. i was a little annoyed but also it's a library, i can't get territorial, that's not the spirit.

the smell of a library is a mix of old paper and slightly damp carpet and whatever cleaning solution they use on the desks. i could pick it out blindfolded. it would make me feel safe even if you dropped me in the strangest city on earth, just to walk into a library and breathe in.

checked out three novels and a biography and i know full well i'll only read one of them but the act of carrying them home in a tote bag feels important. they're a kind of promise. i could read them. they're available to me. the option of them is enough.

the children's section is the loudest part of the library and also somehow the holiest. a kid was sounding out the word 'elephant' phonetically and his mother was so patient. e-luh-fuhnt. e-luh-fuhnt. there's hope for the species in moments like this.

the air conditioner here makes a low hum that is almost meditative. i think they tune libraries to a frequency that helps concentration. or maybe i'm just inventing that because it would explain why i can write here in a way i cannot write at home, where the silence is the wrong shape.

watched someone re-shelve books today and i could have watched it for an hour. they have a cart. they roll it along. they slot each book into its exact correct place. it's like a giant puzzle that resets itself daily. i don't know why this is comforting but it is, deeply.

the library closes at 9 and there's always a small five-minute ritual where the lights blink. you look up from your book. you sigh. you pack your things. you nod at the librarian on the way out. the night outside is sharp and cold and you carry the library with you for an hour after, like incense.

moved my last box in tonight. the apartment is mostly empty. a mattress on the floor. a lamp i bought at the goodwill that has a chipped base. one chair. one fork. one plate. i sat on the floor eating cereal for dinner and felt richer than i've ever felt. nothing in this room belongs to anyone but me.

discovered tonight that the radiator makes a clanking sound at 11pm sharp every night. it's not broken, it's just doing its thing. i'm getting to know all her sounds the way you get to know a new person. the click of the freezer compressor. the soft groan of the floorboards in the hallway. her vocabulary.

first dinner party tonight, sort of. just two friends. we sat on the floor with pizza because i don't have a table yet. it was one of the best nights of my life. there's a particular joy in inviting people into a space that's truly yours for the first time.

bought my first plant for the new apartment. a pothos. small. green. doing her best. i named her phyllis because she looks like a phyllis. i talk to her in the morning while i make coffee. nobody told me a plant would feel like a roommate but here we are.

the freedom to leave a dish in the sink for two days is something i did not know i would value this much. nobody has an opinion. nobody is silently judging. nobody is loudly judging. the dish is in the sink. it is my dish. it is my sink. i'll wash it when i want to.

the building has thin walls and i can hear the woman upstairs do her morning yoga every day at 7am and i don't mind because she also plays beautiful piano in the evenings and i feel like i live above and below the most peaceful person in the city.

the bathtub has feet. did i mention. it has tiny clawed feet like an animal. i did not expect to feel emotional about a piece of plumbing but the bathtub here is older than my grandmother would be if she were alive, and there's something about that continuity that makes me feel like i belong to a longer story.

spent an embarrassing amount of time tonight just looking at the way the streetlight comes in through the kitchen window. it makes a long bright stripe on the floor. it changes when a car drives by. i could watch it for hours. it has become one of the small features of my life.

the loneliness is real, i won't lie. some nights are just silence and i feel it. but then i remember i wanted this. i fought for this. i signed for this. and the silence becomes a different thing. it becomes a room i'm choosing to be in. and that changes everything about how it feels to be in it.

made my bed this morning even though no one was going to see it. i don't know why this feels like a small adult triumph but it does. tucked the corners. fluffed the pillow. stood back. nodded at the bed like a job well done. the bed nodded back, presumably.

the porch faces west which means we get an hour of pure gold light every evening in late august, and then the cicadas start, and then the bats come out, and then the moon shows up like it's been waiting backstage for its cue. it's the best free show in town.

sitting on the porch tonight with a glass of cheap wine and listening to the neighborhood do its evening sounds. someone is grilling. a kid two doors down is learning the violin badly. a dog is barking at something only the dog can see. this is the music i was promised.

you can feel the season turning if you sit out long enough. there's a specific evening in august where the air shifts and suddenly the night has an edge to it. you can smell the fall coming. you put on a sweater for the first time in months. you don't know whether to be sad or relieved.

the porch swing creaks in a rhythm that's two beats slower than my breathing and i'm working on letting my breathing slow down to meet it instead of speeding it up. it's not a competition, the swing has been here longer, the swing knows the pace, i should follow her lead.

a firefly landed on the porch rail tonight and stayed there for almost a full minute, just doing her slow blink, and i swear we were having a conversation. i can't tell you what about. it was the kind of communication that happens between species who don't share words.

the corn from the farm stand is so sweet right now it's almost obscene. ate three ears on the porch with butter dripping down my wrists and didn't even care. there's a small window every year when corn is exactly this good. you miss it if you blink. i don't blink.

watched a thunderstorm roll in from the porch tonight. you could see it for half an hour before it got here. dark line of cloud advancing. the wind picked up. the leaves on the maple flipped silver-side-up. then the first drops, the size of nickels. then the deluge. i didn't go inside. you don't go inside for a show like that.

the neighbor's cat has decided my porch is part of her territory and shows up every evening at 6:30 sharp expecting a small saucer of water and three minutes of attention. she has trained me. she's correct to do so. i have submitted to the routine.

the sound of the screen door slamming behind someone is a specific kind of summer sound. it means a person you love is on their way out to join you. it means iced tea is coming. it means the evening is officially beginning. it means home, in a way that's hard to articulate.

sometimes i think the whole point of having a porch is to give yourself a place to be at the edge of your life. not quite inside, not quite outside. half in the house, half in the world. you sit. you watch. you exist on the threshold. it's a kind of liminal living that everyone deserves.

watched a movie tonight where almost nothing happened for an hour and then a woman cried in a kitchen for ten minutes and i thought it was the best film i've seen all year. that's what i want from indie cinema. people in rooms. the camera not moving. someone finally letting something out.

there's a specific kind of pacing in low-budget movies where you can feel the editor's hand on every cut. they don't have enough coverage. they're making do. and i love this. it makes the film feel like it was made by hands instead of by a committee of agents.

the protagonist of this one was a woman in her forties making bad decisions and the camera just stayed with her, no judgment, no music telling you what to feel. i miss this kind of filmmaking. i miss films that trust you. i miss films that don't pre-chew their emotions for you.

saw something at the festival tonight made by a 23 year old that was genuinely better than half of what gets oscar nominations. shot on what looked like an old digital camera in someone's actual house. four characters. one long weekend. the kind of film that reminds you cinema isn't dead, just looking in a different direction.

the use of natural light in this film is a love language. every interior is dim. every face is half in shadow. it's annoying for fifteen minutes and then your eyes adjust and suddenly you can see what they were going for, and it's beautiful, and you forgive them.

a film that ends with a static shot of a hallway for forty-five seconds is a film that respects you. it says here, sit with it, decide what you think. the hallway means whatever you bring to it. the hallway is the question. the credits roll. you go home. you think about the hallway for a week.

tonight's screening had a q&a after with the director and she said something about how she wrote the screenplay in the year after her father died and you could feel everyone in the theater go still, because suddenly the film made sense, all of it, every choice.

the sound design in this one is incredible. you can hear refrigerators humming. you can hear someone unscrew a jar of pickles three rooms away. it's a film made by people who know that the world is mostly sound, and that you can build mood out of the gentle drone of a furnace.

i don't think the lead actor was a real actor. i think she was the director's actual neighbor. and that's what made it work. the awkward pauses were her actual awkward pauses. you can't pay for that. you can only find it, and ask gently, and pray they say yes.

the final shot of the film tonight was the protagonist standing alone on a beach at dawn for a long minute, not moving, not crying, not doing anything. it was so still you could hear the projector clicking. it shouldn't have worked. it did. that's the magic. that's what i'm always looking for.

spent the afternoon at my kitchen table making collages out of stuff i've been saving in a shoebox. ticket stubs, receipts, a piece of dried flower someone gave me three years ago, the corner of a postcard from my sister. it's not art exactly, it's more like a sentence i can only say with my hands.

found a perfect rusted bottle cap on the sidewalk yesterday and i picked it up like it was a piece of treasure and now it's sitting on my desk waiting to become part of something. i don't know what yet. the bottle cap doesn't know yet either. we're both being patient.

my mother thinks the box of stuff i save is hoarding and my therapist thinks it's a coping mechanism and i think it's actually just art supplies. all three are probably true at the same time, which is how most things work in real life.

today's collage is built around a movie ticket from a date that didn't go well and a leaf from the tree i sit under in the park. you can't tell looking at the finished piece what either thing meant. that's the point. the meaning is composted into the work.

i think the difference between an artist and someone who picks up trash on the sidewalk is the second thing you do after picking up the trash. one person throws it out. one person gives it a new life. nothing else separates us, really.

glued an old library card next to a piece of an envelope my grandfather addressed in 1972. handwriting next to handwriting. two strangers' loops and slants in conversation across decades on my paper. this is what i'm making now. paper conversations between people who never met.

the trick with found object work is to know when to stop. i always want to add one more thing. one more scrap. one more thread. but the moment you add the last thing that should have been the last thing, it stops being art and starts being a pile.

made a tiny collage today inside an altoid tin and gave it to my best friend for her birthday. she cried. i was not expecting her to cry. she put it on her bookshelf and now every time i visit she shows it to whoever else is over. there is no greater compliment for a small piece of art.

i think about all the things i throw away every day and how each of them could have been part of something. it's a kind of mourning. not for the things themselves, but for the alternate universes where i was patient enough to save them, and made something good.

the local art store charges fourteen dollars for what i can find on a single block of any street in this city if i walk slowly enough. the world is making art supplies all the time. you just have to be in the habit of looking down.

third night at the cabin and i've remembered what silence actually sounds like. it's not nothing. it's the sound of snow settling on the roof. it's the soft tick of the woodstove. it's my own breathing, finally slow enough to notice. i forget every time i come up here that this is what i was missing.

split wood for an hour this morning. i'm not good at it. i miss more than i hit. but there's a satisfaction in lining the logs up against the back wall that no office job has ever given me. tangible progress. visible pile. you did this. it'll burn tonight.

the lake froze solid this week and you can hear it groan at night when the temperature drops. low boom sounds, like distant cannons. it's the ice shifting. it scared me the first time. now it sounds like a friend turning over in her sleep in the next room.

made coffee on the woodstove this morning because the propane is out and i couldn't be bothered to drive the forty minutes into town for more. it took an hour. it was the best coffee of my life. i think most of modern life is just paying to skip the part where things take time.

a deer came right up to the porch this evening and stood there looking at me through the window for a long minute. i didn't move. she didn't move. we just looked. then she walked off into the woods like nothing had happened. i'm going to be thinking about that for weeks.

the wind has been coming off the lake for two days and the cabin sounds like a ship. the timbers creak. the windows hum. i sit by the fire and write and feel like a sailor in a story i haven't read yet. the wind doesn't care that i'm here. that's the comfort.

no cell service up here, which i forget every time i come, and which is also the entire reason i come. for three days i don't know what's happening in the world. for three days i don't get notifications. for three days the only news is what the chickadees are doing at the feeder.

tonight the stars are doing the thing where there are too many of them. you forget, living in town, that the sky is supposed to have this many stars. i stood on the porch in my coat and just looked up until my neck hurt. i could pick out the constellations i learned as a kid. they were waiting.

going home tomorrow. i never want to. the trip back down the mountain is the worst part. you can feel yourself getting denser as you descend, the air getting thicker with all the things you'll have to think about again. but i'm taking some of the cabin with me this time. some of the slow. some of the quiet. enough to last until the next visit.
